[{:db/id "knowledge-point-05b40dd4-a99b-5d5e-93b4-767ed99d62a0" :knowledge-point/id #uuid "05b40dd4-a99b-5d5e-93b4-767ed99d62a0" :knowledge-point/canonical-example "question-4ced75f7-e2c9-50f2-b2cf-114222fc960d" :knowledge-point/title "Comparing Two Events by Likelihood" :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e4735ca8-e709-5697-8aaf-f9b52ab3104d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186408190 :topic/knowledge-points ["knowledge-point-05b40dd4-a99b-5d5e-93b4-767ed99d62a0" "knowledge-point-05b40dd4-a99b-5d5e-93b4-767ed99d62a0"] :db/ensure [:topic/identity-validate]} {:db/id "question-4ced75f7-e2c9-50f2-b2cf-114222fc960d" :question/id #uuid "4ced75f7-e2c9-50f2-b2cf-114222fc960d" :question/math-academy-id "e-24942" :question/problem "A scientist records how long it takes for a chemical reaction to complete. The experiment is conducted $40$ times. The table below shows the results.

| Time (seconds) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $<10$ | $6$ |
| $10-20$ | $14$ |
| $20-30$ | $8$ |
| $30-40$ | $7$ |
| $>40$ | $5$ |

Based on the experimental probabilities of these results, complete the following statements.

$\qquad$A reaction completing in more than $30$ seconds is
$\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\phantom{\text{unlikely}}}.$

$\qquad$A reaction completing in less than $20$ seconds is
$\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\phantom{\text{as likely as not}}}.$

$\qquad$A reaction completing in more than $30$ seconds is
$\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\phantom{\text{less likely than}}}$
a reaction completing in less than $20$ seconds." :question/worked-solution "One event is more likely than another if it has a greater probability of occurring. If two events have the same probability, they are equally likely.

Let's consider each statement in turn.

- To compute the experimental probability of a reaction completing in more than $30$ seconds, we divide the number of times a reaction took more than $30$ seconds $(7+5=12)$ by the total number of trials $(40).$ This gives
![](images/41/41ae3b0ee5b77a5967ee949abfd5dc5327fc840e9061cecf1dfd52728405415f.svg)

This probability is a small number, closer to $0.$ Since

$$
0 < \dfrac{3}{10} < \dfrac12,
$$

this event is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{unlikely}}.$

- To compute the experimental probability of a reaction completing in less than $20$ seconds, we divide the number of times a reaction took less than $20$ seconds $(6+14=20)$ by the total number of trials $(40).$ This gives
![](images/19/194542c8095442fe631a733e681d43b025ac5b5f7f478f7b3c541e3c51718c69.svg)

Since the probability is $\dfrac12,$ this event is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{as likely as not}}.$

- The experimental probability of a reaction completing in more than $30$ seconds is less than the experimental probability of a reaction completing in less than $20$ seconds:

$$
\dfrac{3}{10} < \dfrac12.
$$

Therefore, a reaction completing in more than $30$ seconds is
$\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{less likely than}}$
a reaction completing in less than $20$ seconds." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-e4735ca8-e709-5697-8aaf-f9b52ab3104d" :question/id #uuid "e4735ca8-e709-5697-8aaf-f9b52ab3104d" :question/math-academy-id "q-360663" :question/problem "Sarah conducts an experiment $40$ times to see how quickly a machine sorts a bin of parts. The table below shows the results of her experiments.

| Time (seconds) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $<20$ | $6$ |
| $20-30$ | $16$ |
| $30-40$ | $10$ |
| $40-50$ | $5$ |
| $>50$ | $3$ |

Based on the experimental probabilities of these results, complete the following statements.

$\,$A machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds is
{{field-1}}.

$\,$A machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds is
{{field-2}}.

$\,$A machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds is
{{field-3}}
a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds." :question/worked-solution "One event is more likely than another if it has a greater probability of occurring. If two events have the same probability, they are equally likely.

Let's consider each statement in turn.

- To compute the experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds, we divide the number of times a machine sorted a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds $(6+16=22)$ by the total number of times Sarah conducted the experiment $(40).$ This gives

$$
P(\text{sorts in }<30\text{ seconds})=\frac{22}{40}.
$$

This probability is a relatively large number, closer to $1.$ Since

$$
\frac{1}{2}<\frac{22}{40}<1,
$$

this event is $\text{likely}.$

- To compute the experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds, we divide the number of times a machine sorted a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds $(10+5+3=18)$ by the total number of times Sarah conducted the experiment $(40).$ This gives

$$
P(\text{sorts in }>30\text{ seconds})=\frac{18}{40}.
$$

This probability is a small number, closer to $0.$ Since

$$
0<\frac{18}{40}<\frac{1}{2},
$$

this event is $\text{unlikely}.$

- The experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds is *greater than* the experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds:

$$
P(\text{sorts in }<30\text{ seconds})=\frac{22}{40}>\frac{18}{40}=P(\text{sorts in }>30\text{ seconds})
$$

Therefore, a machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds is
$\text{more likely than}$
a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c257aad1-4038-59a0-af10-26f244b309a3" The first few steps of this calculation are shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-1+h)-f(-1)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(-1+h)^{2}-(-1)^{2}}{h} \\  & =…\end{aligned}
$$

Finish the calculation, and hence find ${f}^{′}(-1).$" :question/worked-solution "By proceeding with the remaining calculations we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-1+h)-f(-1)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(-1+h)^{2}-(-1)^{2}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1-2h+{h}^{2}-1}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{h(-2+h)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(-2+h) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(-1)=-2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-26e0a8d8-3d22-5a55-a37b-cb46b000140b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/worked-solution "*Method 1:*

By the definition, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(1)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}.
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=5{x}^{2}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{5(1+h)^{2}-5(1)^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{5+10h+5{h}^{2}-5}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{10h+5{h}^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(10+5h) \\  & =10+(0) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

 

*Method 2:*

By the definition, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(1)={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)-f(1)}{x-1}.
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=5{x}^{2}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & ={lim}_{x\to 1}(\frac{5{x}^{2}-5(1)^{2}}{x-1}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}(\frac{5({x}^{2}-1)}{x-1}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}(\frac{5(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}5(x+1) \\  & =5(1+1) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-140d3701-ba23-5c26-9cf9-6d695b5d1f47"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/id #uuid "f0b66b9d-4d88-5de4-a9f2-e4468c8b8ed2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163105" :question/problem "For the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)=\sqrt{x+y+4},$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=2+ax+\frac{1}{4}y-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{2}+bxy+c{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y+4}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y+4}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =\frac{1}{4}, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32} \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32} \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈2+\frac{1}{4}\cdot x+\frac{1}{4}\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{32}\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-\frac{1}{32})\cdot xy+(-\frac{1}{32})\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =2+\frac{1}{4}x+\frac{1}{4}y-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{2}+(-\frac{1}{32})xy+(-\frac{1}{64}){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=\frac{1}{4}+(-\frac{1}{32})+(-\frac{1}{64})=\frac{13}{64}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-57708cab-0a02-5b87-93ec-6746644b7829"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-57708cab-0a02-5b87-93ec-6746644b7829" :answer-field/id #uuid "57708cab-0a02-5b87-93ec-6746644b7829" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b5cff024-e8a3-5830-b01f-71c191133afb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b5cff024-e8a3-5830-b01f-71c191133afb" "answer-213c31e4-604c-5637-a050-4eaeb6c0f751" "answer-b6db8036-e893-58df-8210-1dab0e50bf02" "answer-878b145b-533e-56a3-a50a-7a45a1f3deec" "answer-cb9dc1c3-ffa1-5373-bb29-a4874096f214"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b5cff024-e8a3-5830-b01f-71c191133afb" :answer/id #uuid "b5cff024-e8a3-5830-b01f-71c191133afb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{13}{64}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-213c31e4-604c-5637-a050-4eaeb6c0f751" :answer/id #uuid "213c31e4-604c-5637-a050-4eaeb6c0f751" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{15}{32}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b6db8036-e893-58df-8210-1dab0e50bf02" :answer/id #uuid "b6db8036-e893-58df-8210-1dab0e50bf02" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{25}{64}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-878b145b-533e-56a3-a50a-7a45a1f3deec" :answer/id #uuid "878b145b-533e-56a3-a50a-7a45a1f3deec" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{16}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cb9dc1c3-ffa1-5373-bb29-a4874096f214" :answer/id #uuid "cb9dc1c3-ffa1-5373-bb29-a4874096f214" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{9}{32}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-983968fc-15f6-5756-ab92-7399b778fa93" :question/id #uuid "983968fc-15f6-5756-ab92-7399b778fa93" :question/math-academy-id "q-163108" :question/problem "For the function of two variables

$$

$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x+{e}^{y}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{{e}^{y}}{x+{e}^{y}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =1, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\frac{{e}^{y}}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{x{e}^{y}}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈0+1\cdot x+1\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-1)\cdot xy+0\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1x+1y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+(-1)xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1+1+(-1)=1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-be0946b1-502a-5aba-b006-539568a4bc82"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables. Find the conditional expected value $\textrm{E}\big[Y \,|\, X=1\big]$ given that the conditional probability density function $f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, 1)$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\textrm E\big[ Y \,|\, X = x \big] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y \, f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, x) \; \textrm{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{9}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162127 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b25c780b-4145-5bfa-8e04-0856e9d67d3a" "question-28a2968a-07fa-5df6-a93c-3d505caa4a83" "question-4aa42e03-e8d1-5333-8d07-d9074e34a91f" "question-13aa670b-3e27-50cc-b24b-f562a4443719" "question-b86ab1d5-8833-598a-9757-b29ccf7f9acc"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161693 :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}y-x, & -1\le x\le 0,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+y, & 0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\textrm{E}\bigg[X \,\bigg|\, Y=\dfrac{1}{2} \bigg].$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\textrm E\big[ X \,|\, Y = y \big] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, f_{X|Y}(x \,|\, y) \; \textrm{d}x.
$$

Note that $\textrm E\big[ X \,|\, Y = y \big]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{y-x}{\frac{1}{2}+y} \\  & =\frac{2(y-x)}{1+2y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $-1 \leq x \leq 0, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1.$ Outside this domain, we have $f_{X|Y} (x \,|\, y) = 0.$

Now, substituting $y=\dfrac{1}{2}$ into the expression for $f_{X|Y} (x \,|\, y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2}) & =\frac{2(\frac{1}{2}-x)}{1+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-2x}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=\frac{1}{2}] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}x(\frac{1}{2}-x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(\frac{x}{2}-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{7}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162128 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4a9126d5-9f56-54dd-b358-d393eac16b93" "question-200b9c27-2539-5e86-b17a-fa5314a06310" "question-7abac60c-426c-5228-9bff-bdb217864577" "question-5142c769-0ab4-5c62-90f2-d5f937ec0c66" "question-4c1f6156-411f-54e4-bb68-bbf84af25120"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161694 :question/problem "$$

$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\textrm{E}\big[Y \,|\, X=x\big]$ for $0 <     x <     2.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\textrm E\big[ Y \,|\, X = x \big] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y \, f_{Y|X}(y \,|\, x) \; \textrm{d}y.
$$

Note that $\textrm E\big[ Y \,|\, X = x \big]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{x+y}{4})}{(\frac{3{x}^{2}}{8})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+y)}{3{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \leq y \leq x,\; 0 <              x <             2.$ Outside this domain, we have $f_{Y|X} (y \,|\, x) = 0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{x}y\cdot \,\frac{2(x+y)}{3{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{x}(xy+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3{x}^{2}}{[\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{x} \\  & =\frac{2}{3{x}^{2}}[\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-0] \\  & =\frac{2}{3{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{5{x}^{3}}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{3{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{5{x}^{2}\cdot x}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cancel{{x}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{5\cancel{{x}^{2}}\cdot x}{3} \\  & =\frac{5x}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-db6164d4-0ab9-5b8d-a944-50886d9aea3b" :question/id #uuid "db6164d4-0ab9-5b8d-a944-50886d9aea3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-146180" :question/problem "$$

Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=2]$ given that the conditional probability density function ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=2] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x\cdot \frac{x}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{12}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{27}{12}-\frac{1}{12} \\  & =\frac{13}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186159704 :answer-field/correct 17592186159708 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-b25c780b-4145-5bfa-8e04-0856e9d67d3a" :question/id #uuid "b25c780b-4145-5bfa-8e04-0856e9d67d3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-146253" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+3y}{12}, & 1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y+1}{4}, & 0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1].$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2x+3y}{12})}{(\frac{y+1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{2x+3y}{3y+3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{2x+3\cdot 1}{3\cdot 1+3}=\frac{2x+3}{6}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{2x+3}{6}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{1}^{2}(2{x}^{2}+3x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}((\frac{16}{3}+6)-(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{2})) \\  & =\frac{55}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ce1f1101-3df3-5c9e-9c08-818c39307178"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ce1f1101-3df3-5c9e-9c08-818c39307178" :answer-field/id #uuid "ce1f1101-3df3-5c9e-9c08-818c39307178" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4661b057-e34b-5ad1-86ad-f2170ff87ca2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ef193c69-7a43-5081-98b8-a77c6b8cc73b" "answer-1ddc283e-0948-540b-b84c-d2835daf8f6f" "answer-416e4a5c-22d6-5be2-bec7-c3eae49ba017" "answer-0d6fd54d-4c1c-55c6-8760-81621dbc6cde" "answer-4661b057-e34b-5ad1-86ad-f2170ff87ca2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ef193c69-7a43-5081-98b8-a77c6b8cc73b" :answer/id #uuid "ef193c69-7a43-5081-98b8-a77c6b8cc73b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1ddc283e-0948-540b-b84c-d2835daf8f6f" :answer/id #uuid "1ddc283e-0948-540b-b84c-d2835daf8f6f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{14}{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-416e4a5c-22d6-5be2-bec7-c3eae49ba017" :answer/id #uuid "416e4a5c-22d6-5be2-bec7-c3eae49ba017" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{25}{18}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0d6fd54d-4c1c-55c6-8760-81621dbc6cde" :answer/id #uuid "0d6fd54d-4c1c-55c6-8760-81621dbc6cde" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{31}{18}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4661b057-e34b-5ad1-86ad-f2170ff87ca2" :answer/id #uuid "4661b057-e34b-5ad1-86ad-f2170ff87ca2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{55}{36}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-28a2968a-07fa-5df6-a93c-3d505caa4a83" :question/id #uuid "28a2968a-07fa-5df6-a93c-3d505caa4a83" :question/math-academy-id "q-146345" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}12xy, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}6{x}^{5}, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1].$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as  

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{12xy}{6{x}^{5}} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{4}},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0<x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|1\,)=2y.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot (2y)\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}

Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1].$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(2-x-y)}{(\frac{3}{2}-y)} \\  & =\frac{4-2x-2y}{3-2y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{4-2x-2\cdot 1}{3-2\cdot 1}=\frac{4-2x-2}{3-2}=2-2x.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(2-2x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x-2{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ for $0<x<1.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6(x+y)}{5})}{3{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+y)}{5{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x\le y\le 2x,\,0<x<1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{x}^{2x}y\cdot \,\frac{2(x+y)}{5{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{5{x}^{2}}{\int }_{x}^{2x}(xy+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{5{x}^{2}}{[\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{x}^{2x} \\  & =\frac{2}{5{x}^{2}}[(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{8{x}^{3}}{3})-(\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})] \\  & =\frac{2}{5{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{23{x}^{3}}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cancel{{x}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{23x\cdot \cancel{({x}^{2})}}{3} \\  & =\frac{23x}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8f740bd4-a687-5983-91a3-7513fe971934"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8f740bd4-a687-5983-91a3-7513fe971934" :answer-field/id #uuid "8f740bd4-a687-5983-91a3-7513fe971934" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-fa62812a-5ad0-5c54-8abe-7a6dfef958dc" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fa62812a-5ad0-5c54-8abe-7a6dfef958dc" "answer-da064ca0-ec2d-5668-b781-affcc343f33c" "answer-b9ece17e-ce07-5a63-9272-3986c9fc0b28" "answer-49e3ff31-b227-5b2a-8fe3-d34a74248ace" "answer-8262ba09-25dc-5226-a050-4bcaa05979b4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fa62812a-5ad0-5c54-8abe-7a6dfef958dc" :answer/id #uuid "fa62812a-5ad0-5c54-8abe-7a6dfef958dc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{23x}{15}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-da064ca0-ec2d-5668-b781-affcc343f33c" :answer/id #uuid "da064ca0-ec2d-5668-b781-affcc343f33c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2x+y}{15}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b9ece17e-ce07-5a63-9272-3986c9fc0b28" :answer/id #uuid "b9ece17e-ce07-5a63-9272-3986c9fc0b28" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2{x}^{2}}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-49e3ff31-b227-5b2a-8fe3-d34a74248ace" :answer/id #uuid "49e3ff31-b227-5b2a-8fe3-d34a74248ace" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3{x}^{2}}{15}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8262ba09-25dc-5226-a050-4bcaa05979b4" :answer/id #uuid "8262ba09-25dc-5226-a050-4bcaa05979b4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{x+y}{15}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7abac60c-426c-5228-9bff-bdb217864577" :question/id #uuid "7abac60c-426c-5228-9bff-bdb217864577" :question/math-academy-id "q-146397" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3x{y}^{2}}{4}, & 0\le y\le 2,\,0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x, & 0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ for $0<x<1.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3x{y}^{2}}{4})}{2x} \\  & =\frac{3{y}^{2}}{8},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le y\le 2,\,0<x<1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y\cdot \,\frac{3{y}^{2}}{8}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{8}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{8}{[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{8}[4-0] \\  & =\frac{3}{8}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3a063c31-7ea1-511c-9093-dca00ca75be6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3a063c31-7ea1-511c-9093-dca00ca75be6" :answer-field/id #uuid "3a063c31-7ea1-511c-9093-dca00ca75be6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-51d6868e-9f63-566b-8657-3e46a79dcf7f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4b7b8be0-cd7d-5f2a-8d07-58b09b3e02bd" "answer-a358ba73-65d0-5ebe-ae65-bacd7eb25e86" "answer-cf07accb-49d6-5bf1-b6e5-cfad1ed38be2" "answer-51d6868e-9f63-566b-8657-3e46a79dcf7f" "answer-a6fae95c-8607-5baf-bcfe-438d0e382039"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b7b8be0-cd7d-5f2a-8d07-58b09b3e02bd" :answer/id #uuid "4b7b8be0-cd7d-5f2a-8d07-58b09b3e02bd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a358ba73-65d0-5ebe-ae65-bacd7eb25e86" :answer/id #uuid "a358ba73-65d0-5ebe-ae65-bacd7eb25e86" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cf07accb-49d6-5bf1-b6e5-cfad1ed38be2" :answer/id #uuid "cf07accb-49d6-5bf1-b6e5-cfad1ed38be2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-51d6868e-9f63-566b-8657-3e46a79dcf7f" :answer/id #uuid "51d6868e-9f63-566b-8657-3e46a79dcf7f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a6fae95c-8607-5baf-bcfe-438d0e382039" :answer/id #uuid "a6fae95c-8607-5baf-bcfe-438d0e382039" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5142c769-0ab4-5c62-90f2-d5f937ec0c66" :question/id #uuid "5142c769-0ab4-5c62-90f2-d5f937ec0c66" :question/math-academy-id "q-146538" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2(x+2y)}{3}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1+4y}{3}, & 0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ for $0\le y\le 1.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2(x+2y)}{3})}{(\frac{1+4y}{3})} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \,\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+2yx)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+y{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}\cdot [\frac{1}{3}+y-0] \\  & =\frac{2}{1+4y}\cdot \frac{1+3y}{3} \\  & =\frac{2(1+3y)}{3(1+4y)}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e1a039c4-3510-5a92-9df7-feb0d8d5d857"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e1a039c4-3510-5a92-9df7-feb0d8d5d857" :answer-field/id #uuid "e1a039c4-3510-5a92-9df7-feb0d8d5d857" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-db470a65-0a51-550a-8ffd-cf65f10f85a6" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5345dbd5-7e99-5317-8490-c789146a8788" "answer-e1e56427-f6a7-5af0-99d9-80933b07e001" "answer-1bf9c026-9fde-556b-a693-fbda3046a227" "answer-46d79442-5892-5af0-818d-d2ead962340e" "answer-db470a65-0a51-550a-8ffd-cf65f10f85a6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5345dbd5-7e99-5317-8490-c789146a8788" :answer/id #uuid "5345dbd5-7e99-5317-8490-c789146a8788" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{(1+3y)}{(1+4y)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e1e56427-f6a7-5af0-99d9-80933b07e001" :answer/id #uuid "e1e56427-f6a7-5af0-99d9-80933b07e001" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{(1+3y)}{3(1+4y)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1bf9c026-9fde-556b-a693-fbda3046a227" :answer/id #uuid "1bf9c026-9fde-556b-a693-fbda3046a227" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{(1+4y)}{(1+3y)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-46d79442-5892-5af0-818d-d2ead962340e" :answer/id #uuid "46d79442-5892-5af0-818d-d2ead962340e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{(y+3)}{3(y+4)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-db470a65-0a51-550a-8ffd-cf65f10f85a6" :answer/id #uuid "db470a65-0a51-550a-8ffd-cf65f10f85a6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2(1+3y)}{3(1+4y)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-4c1f6156-411f-54e4-bb68-bbf84af25120" :question/id #uuid "4c1f6156-411f-54e4-bb68-bbf84af25120" :question/math-academy-id "q-146520" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{5}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,0<y<1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{6y+2}{5}, & 0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ for $0<y<1.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{5})}{(\frac{6y+2}{5})} \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{6y+2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \,\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{6y+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}+xy)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{2}y}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}[\frac{1}{4}+\frac{y}{2}-0] \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}\cdot \frac{1+2y}{4} \\  & =\frac{6}{2(3y+1)}\cdot \frac{(1+2y)}{4} \\  & =\frac{3(1+2y)}{4(3y+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3d5798b6-1edf-5ed2-bbb7-aae35b6bf653"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3d5798b6-1edf-5ed2-bbb7-aae35b6bf653" :answer-field/id #uuid "3d5798b6-1edf-5ed2-bbb7-aae35b6bf653" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-445f339a-c1d1-5908-9ed9-b51956b4aff3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-73ea5849-0a8b-5581-9a68-493551edf6c6" "answer-1ccc6750-246a-5a6e-8d0b-5e04b2fcec20" "answer-8bf1aa4b-de93-56ed-90a9-5e53ffe6181a" "answer-445f339a-c1d1-5908-9ed9-b51956b4aff3" "answer-c6a557fd-77df-511c-836c-c00052e9bf42"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-73ea5849-0a8b-5581-9a68-493551edf6c6" :answer/id #uuid "73ea5849-0a8b-5581-9a68-493551edf6c6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{(1+2y)}{(3y+1)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1ccc6750-246a-5a6e-8d0b-5e04b2fcec20" :answer/id #uuid "1ccc6750-246a-5a6e-8d0b-5e04b2fcec20" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{(1+2y)}{4(3y+1)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8bf1aa4b-de93-56ed-90a9-5e53ffe6181a" :answer/id #uuid "8bf1aa4b-de93-56ed-90a9-5e53ffe6181a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2y}{2(3y+1)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-445f339a-c1d1-5908-9ed9-b51956b4aff3" :answer/id #uuid "445f339a-c1d1-5908-9ed9-b51956b4aff3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3(1+2y)}{4(3y+1)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c6a557fd-77df-511c-836c-c00052e9bf42" :answer/id #uuid "c6a557fd-77df-511c-836c-c00052e9bf42" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3{y}^{2}}{4(y+3)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163340 :tutorial/content "For continuous random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the **conditional expectation of $X$ given $Y=y$** is defined as

$$
\textrm E[X |Y = y] =\int\limits_{\mathbb R} x \, f_{X|Y}(x|y)\;\textrm dx,
$$

where $f_{X|Y}(x|y)$ is the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y.$ 

This definition is similar to that of $\textrm{E}[X].$ However, we now use the conditional PDF $f_{X|Y}(x|y)$ instead of the marginal PDF $f_X(x)$ in our integral.

Note the following:

- When we select a particular value of $y,$ the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ returns a real number. However, if $y$ is not specified, i.e., $\textrm{E}[X |Y = y]$ *depends* on $y,$ we have that $\textrm{E}[X |Y = y]$ gives us a *function* of $y.$

- If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\textrm E[X | Y = y] = \textrm E[X]$ for all $y$.

- We sometimes use the notation $\mu_{X|y}$ to denote $E[X | Y = y].$

- We have an analogous definition for $\textrm E[Y |X = x]\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm E[Y |X = x] =\int\limits_{\mathbb R} y \, f_{Y|X}(y|x)\;\textrm dy,
$$

where $f_{Y|X}(y|x)$ is the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163348 :tutorial/content "Let's find the conditional expectation $\textrm{E}\big[X \,|\, Y=1\big]$ given that the conditional probability density function $f_{X|Y}(x \,|\, 1)$ is given by
![](images/8b/8b71da7aecae81ed4e8d9dc27f4730d3d0a03d73146b7b899003d3f8787694bc.svg) 

Applying the formula for the conditional expectation of $X$ given $Y=y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot 2(x-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x(x-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2{x}^{2}-2x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}-{x}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{2(2)^{3}}{3}-(2)^{2}]-[\frac{2(1)^{3}}{3}-(1)^{2}] \\  & =[\frac{16}{3}-4]-[\frac{2}{3}-1] \\  & =[\frac{16}{3}-\frac{12}{3}]-[\frac{2}{3}-\frac{3}{3}] \\  & =\frac{4}{3}-(-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162193 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100825 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-862b92b4-3ae1-5d18-841c-0f1c9c5cb6ec" "question-a12bbd8d-9dfc-5edb-a067-bd2603dd76bf"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-862b92b4-3ae1-5d18-841c-0f1c9c5cb6ec" :question/id #uuid "862b92b4-3ae1-5d18-841c-0f1c9c5cb6ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-20254" :question/problem "![](images/42/42e163dd119aaea37d2a373310b408a409023400a6f84ff520c464c6acb153b9.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)?$" :question/worked-solution "Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y=f(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,0.3)$ | $0.3$ | $(0.3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |

Additionally, the function has an inflection point at $x≈-0.3.$ So ${f}^{″}(-0.3)≈0$ and the tangent to the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis.

We don't know the exact value of ${f}^{′}(-0.3)$ but from the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that at $x≈-0.3,$ the slope is positive.

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$" :question/worked-solution "Since the function is piecewise-linear, we get a constant derivative over each linear part.
Notice the following:

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we get ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

- When $f(x)$ is constant, we get ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $\text{const.}$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $\text{undef.}$ | $0$ |

From the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points. 

Additionally, we have a change of the slope of the tangent line (from negative to $0$) when we pass through $x=4$ from left to right. This means that the derivative is not defined at $x=4$ and we obtain a jump discontinuity at this point for the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x).$

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y=f(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |

Additionally, the function has an inflection point at $x≈0.$ So ${f}^{″}(0)≈0$ and the tangent to the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis.

We don't know the exact value of ${f}^{′}(0)$ but from the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that at $x≈0,$ the slope is positive.

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

The graph of the function $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $y=f(x)$, is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{″}(x)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, if we denote $g(x)={f}^{′}(x)$ then ${f}^{″}(x)={g}^{′}(x).$ So, we need to sketch the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$ given the graph of $y=g(x),$ as usual.

Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=g(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${g}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $g(x)$ is increasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $g(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $g$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |
| ${g}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Additionally, the function $y=g(x)$ has inflection points at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5.$ At the inflection points, we have ${g}^{″}(x)=0,$ so the tangent to the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5.$ 

We don't know the exact values of ${g}^{′}(-0.5)$ and ${g}^{′}(0.5)$, but from the graph of $y=g(x)$ we find that the slope of the tangents to ${g}^{′}(x)$ at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5$ are positive and negative, respectively.  

Therefore, the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)={f}^{″}(x)$ may look as shown below.

{:db/id 17592186125083 :question/problem "Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1,$ and determine which of the following statements is true." :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y+1=0 \\ x+3y+5=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
2y+4=0\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
x+(-2)+1=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Hence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get

$$
H(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186123098 :answer-field/correct "answer-23d7c23e-2e7c-57ed-a669-10ce3af13e38" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fe0c6bef-702a-5967-84e7-559ce04a5279" "answer-4396e4d8-a763-52af-afef-ded9f6e55a26" "answer-1caf69dd-971a-5d35-89cb-d9626dcb78d5" "answer-23d7c23e-2e7c-57ed-a669-10ce3af13e38" "answer-2c29ee3e-35ef-5627-a600-d2e0619b9541"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fe0c6bef-702a-5967-84e7-559ce04a5279" :answer/id #uuid "fe0c6bef-702a-5967-84e7-559ce04a5279" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(-3,2)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4396e4d8-a763-52af-afef-ded9f6e55a26" :answer/id #uuid "4396e4d8-a763-52af-afef-ded9f6e55a26" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local maximum at $(1,-2)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1caf69dd-971a-5d35-89cb-d9626dcb78d5" :answer/id #uuid "1caf69dd-971a-5d35-89cb-d9626dcb78d5" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(-3,2)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-23d7c23e-2e7c-57ed-a669-10ce3af13e38" :answer/id #uuid "23d7c23e-2e7c-57ed-a669-10ce3af13e38" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2c29ee3e-35ef-5627-a600-d2e0619b9541" :answer/id #uuid "2c29ee3e-35ef-5627-a600-d2e0619b9541" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(1,-2)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125084 :question/problem "Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-6y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}-6x.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y=0 \\ 3{y}^{2}-6x=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
3{x}^{2}-6y=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})}^{2}-6x & =0 \\ \frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-2x & =0 \\ {x}^{4}-8x & =0 \\ x({x}^{3}-8) & =0 \\ x & =0,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
x=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}=0,\,\,x=2\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}=2.
$$

Hence, $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=6x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=-6 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=-6\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=6y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6x & -6 \\ -6 & 6y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))=0\cdot 0-(-6)^{2}=-36<0.
$$

Therefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(2,2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(2,2)=[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 \\ -6 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(2,2),$ we get

$$
H(2,2)=det({f}^{″}(2,2))=12\cdot 12-(-6)^{2}=108>0.
$$

Finally, since $H(2,2)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(2,2)=({f}^{″}(2,2))_{11}=12>0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(2,2).$

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(2,2).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186123104 "60652dd5-fdd9-5974-9d65-a71597afa3f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-104994" :question/problem "The function 
$f(x,y)$
has the first derivative

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],
$$

and has a stationary point at $(3,-3).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $H(3,-3)>0$

II. $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)<0$

III. The point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4x+2y-6,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+2y-6)=4 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+2y)=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,-3),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,-3)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(3,-3),$ we get

$$
H(3,-3)=det({f}^{″}(3,-3))=4\cdot 2-{2}^{2}=4>0.
$$

- Statement II is false. We have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)=({f}^{″}(3,-3))_{11}=4>0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(3,-3)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)>0,$ the point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-06c9a2bb-e41c-52c6-8b2c-a83b5dffeaf4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-06c9a2bb-e41c-52c6-8b2c-a83b5dffeaf4" :answer-field/id #uuid "06c9a2bb-e41c-52c6-8b2c-a83b5dffeaf4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3bef4c65-0c4b-5059-b575-1485beb2844b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d30d25a2-0e79-557a-a62e-539de549b8be" "answer-3bef4c65-0c4b-5059-b575-1485beb2844b" "answer-2b6b1671-0717-5482-8d52-d0c250e890fe" "answer-862feb99-123c-5810-b1cc-80efe435e8f0" "answer-63cd11be-33ac-578f-99a4-b5fbfef6ba96"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d30d25a2-0e79-557a-a62e-539de549b8be" :answer/id #uuid "d30d25a2-0e79-557a-a62e-539de549b8be" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3bef4c65-0c4b-5059-b575-1485beb2844b" :answer/id #uuid "3bef4c65-0c4b-5059-b575-1485beb2844b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2b6b1671-0717-5482-8d52-d0c250e890fe" :answer/id #uuid "2b6b1671-0717-5482-8d52-d0c250e890fe" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-862feb99-123c-5810-b1cc-80efe435e8f0" :answer/id #uuid "862feb99-123c-5810-b1cc-80efe435e8f0" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-63cd11be-33ac-578f-99a4-b5fbfef6ba96" :answer/id #uuid "63cd11be-33ac-578f-99a4-b5fbfef6ba96" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-f7f93cc0-fc36-5de6-903e-61c89b0db59c" :question/id #uuid "f7f93cc0-fc36-5de6-903e-61c89b0db59c" :question/math-academy-id "q-105213" :question/problem "The function 
$f(x,y)$
has the first derivative

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}],
$$

and has a stationary point at $(-1,1).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $H(-1,1)<0$

II. $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)<0$

III. The point $(-1,1)$ is a local maximum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})=\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & -\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(-1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-1,1)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(-1,1),$ we get

$$
H(-1,1)=det({f}^{″}(-1,1))=(-2)^{2}-(-1)^{2}=3>0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)=({f}^{″}(-1,1))_{11}=-2<0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(-1,1)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)<0,$ the point $(-1,1)$ is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6b0046f1-2976-582a-85ca-24a28e09b21d"] :db/ensure :question/worked-solution "First, we substitute $t=10$ into the function. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{3})-\operatorname{log}⁡(10t) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{3})-\operatorname{log}⁡(10\cdot 10) \\  & =2\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{3})-\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

The common logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=3$ and $x=2.$ Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{3})-\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{2})=2\cdot 3-2=4\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-89a053ca-7dc5-596c-888f-925fbf0bae39"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-89a053ca-7dc5-596c-888f-925fbf0bae39" :answer-field/id #uuid "89a053ca-7dc5-596c-888f-925fbf0bae39" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-abb0d127-729c-52ec-899c-f4b419e34c74" :answer-field/choices ["answer-35a1c537-1707-54d3-98ae-af863b9980c7" "answer-36c63ad2-e5ab-5c30-950c-3e5928c6abe8" "answer-97afabea-2893-5176-8db1-49f34160a9b0" "answer-b1e80a2a-2a90-5e03-8332-b82cf6f8f572" "answer-abb0d127-729c-52ec-899c-f4b419e34c74"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-35a1c537-1707-54d3-98ae-af863b9980c7" :answer/id #uuid "35a1c537-1707-54d3-98ae-af863b9980c7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-36c63ad2-e5ab-5c30-950c-3e5928c6abe8" :answer/id #uuid "36c63ad2-e5ab-5c30-950c-3e5928c6abe8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-97afabea-2893-5176-8db1-49f34160a9b0" :answer/id #uuid "97afabea-2893-5176-8db1-49f34160a9b0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1e80a2a-2a90-5e03-8332-b82cf6f8f572" :answer/id #uuid "b1e80a2a-2a90-5e03-8332-b82cf6f8f572" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-abb0d127-729c-52ec-899c-f4b419e34c74" :answer/id #uuid "abb0d127-729c-52ec-899c-f4b419e34c74" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233673 :question/problem "Find the value of $\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{2})+\operatorname{log}⁡(10t)$ at $t=10.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we substitute $t=10$ into the function. $$

$$
\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x})=x

In our example, we have

$$
\log(100)=\log_{10}(100)=\log_{10}(10^2) = 2.
$$

In general, the logarithm with base $10$ is called the **common logarithm**, and is defined as follows:

$a = 10^x$ is equivalent to $\log{a} = x$

Everything we did with logarithms, we can do with the common logarithm. For example, we can

- convert between exponential and logarithm form,

- evaluate common logarithm expressions, and

- calculate specific values of $\log a$ using a calculator.

Finally, note that most calculators have a button for the common logarithm. "7e900458-4a34-53b2-8b6d-fd38c3b57268" :question/math-academy-id "q-125986" :question/problem "Using the definition of the hyperbolic cosine, calculate ${f}^{-1}(x)$ given that $f(x)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)$ and $x\ge -1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $y=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1).$ Since $x\ge -1,$ we have $y\ge 1.$

To find the inverse function we swap $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
x=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(y+1),
$$

where $x\ge 1$ and $y\ge -1.$

Next, we apply the definition of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{y+1}+{e}^{-(y+1)}) \\ 2x & ={e}^{y+1}+{e}^{-(y+1)} \\ 2x{e}^{y+1} & ={e}^{2(y+1)}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Bringing everything to the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(y+1)}-2x{e}^{y+1}+1 & =0 \\ {({e}^{y+1})}^{2}-2x({e}^{y+1})+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Y={e}^{y+1}.$ We can form a quadratic equation in $Y$ and solve it by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Y}^{2}-2xY+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2}-{x}^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ Y-x & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ Y & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ {e}^{y+1} & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ y+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for  $x\ge 1,$ we have $x-\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\le 1$ and  $x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\ge 1.$ Since $y+1\ge 0,$ the logarithm in the above equality must be non-negative. This requires its argument to be greater than or equal to $1$ for $x\ge 1$, so we reject the alternative with the negative sign. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

:question/problem "Given the elliptic cone $\frac{(x-6)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{8}=(z-2)^{2},$ find its intercepts with the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "To find the $x$-intercepts of the elliptic cone, we plug $y=0$ and $z=0$ into the equation and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-6)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(0-4)^{2}}{8} & =(0-2)^{2} \\ \frac{(x-6)^{2}}{2}+\frac{16}{8} & =4 \\ \frac{(x-6)^{2}}{2}+2 & =4 \\ \frac{(x-6)^{2}}{2} & =2 \\ (x-6)^{2} & =4 \\ x-6 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =6\pm 2 \\ x & =4,8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $x$-axis are $(4,0,0)$ and $(8,0,0).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7b271f10-b638-58d9-8c15-6f54a2760bc2"] "question-bfa27842-a6ff-52d4-867b-7142afc0e5fe"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078199 :question/problem "Find the common ratio of the following geometric sequence.

$$
90, \: -30, \: 10, \: -\dfrac{10}{3}, \: \ldots
$$" :question/worked-solution "The common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence is the constant we multiply by to get to the next term. In other words, it is the ratio of consecutive terms.

Therefore, the common ratio for our sequence is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{(-30)}{90} = -\dfrac{1}{3}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078545 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-feb40554-9f62-5369-873c-1a4212bcc47c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078200 :question/problem "Find the $7$th term of the following geometric sequence.

$$
1, \: 2, \: 4, \: 8, \: \ldots
$$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/65/653f9ccfe28f5e3630afd30562064f1d790245b227896ea7db2da4265f7bac1a.png)

Notice that the sequence is geometric, with a common ratio of 

$$
r=\dfrac{2}{1}=2.
$$

So, we can get each term by multiplying the previous term by $2.$

Continuing to list terms of the sequence until we get to the $7$th term, we obtain the following:

![](images/6a/6ae31d38f90d943b5bd802652d0dedd4925351b1ffadd6398d018a1dd4c7f0d3.png)

Therefore, the $7$th term is $64.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078546 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-aefd99db-cf1d-5552-bc9d-e8816ab40f33" "question-2e89be9b-05fd-570e-aab3-708af6042f1b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078214 :question/problem "Given that $x$, $3x$, $36$ are the first three terms of a geometric sequence, find $x.$" :question/worked-solution "The first three terms are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=x,\,{a}_{2}=3x,\,{a}_{3}=36.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{3x}{x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{36}{3x}=\frac{12}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =\frac{12}{x} \\ 3x & =12 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078547 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5bf4971e-04f4-56ea-b8f7-ec174707b886" "question-011f3c60-0a40-5c48-8e42-7ae45f302869"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078201 :question/problem "Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $2, \: 4, \: 8, \: 16, \: \ldots$

II. $1, \: -\dfrac{1}{3}, \: \dfrac{1}{9}, \: -\dfrac{1}{27}, \: \ldots$

III. $4, \: 8, \: 12, \: 16, \: \ldots$" :question/worked-solution "A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{4}{2} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{8}{4} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}}=\frac{16}{8} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is also geometric. Again, for each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{(-\frac{1}{3})}{1} & =-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{(\frac{1}{9})}{(-\frac{1}{3})} & =-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}}=\frac{(-\frac{1}{27})}{(\frac{1}{9})} & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{8}{4} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{12}{8} & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequences I and II could be geometric sequences." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-5d70384a-18d5-5ae8-aba3-5e0332c40c5f" :question/id #uuid "5d70384a-18d5-5ae8-aba3-5e0332c40c5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-250656" :question/problem "Consider the following geometric sequence:

$$
243,\,-162,\,108,\,-72,\,…
$$

The common ratio of this geometric sequence is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "The common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence is the constant we multiply by to get to the next term. In other words, it is the ratio of consecutive terms.

Therefore, the common ratio for our sequence is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{(-162)}{243}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-34a2f5ca-3647-52a4-8e96-552ff18e0cf0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-34a2f5ca-3647-52a4-8e96-552ff18e0cf0" :answer-field/id #uuid "34a2f5ca-3647-52a4-8e96-552ff18e0cf0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-a94638c3-3706-5557-8410-7e36882e8a69" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a94638c3-3706-5557-8410-7e36882e8a69"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a94638c3-3706-5557-8410-7e36882e8a69" :answer/id #uuid "a94638c3-3706-5557-8410-7e36882e8a69" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-bfa27842-a6ff-52d4-867b-7142afc0e5fe" :question/id #uuid "bfa27842-a6ff-52d4-867b-7142afc0e5fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-250632" :question/problem "Consider the following geometric sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=8,\,{a}_{2}=6x,\,{a}_{3}=10x.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{6x}{8}=\frac{3x}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{10x}{6x}=\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x}{4} & =\frac{5}{3} \\ 3x & =\frac{20}{3} \\ x & =\frac{20}{9}.\end{aligned}

I. $-1,\,-6,\,-36,\,…$

II. $1,\,-4,\,-16,\,…$

III. $2,\,7,\,12,\,…$" :question/worked-solution "A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-6)}{(-1)}=6 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-36)}{(-6)}=6\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-4)}{1}=-4 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-16)}{(-4)}=4\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is also not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{7}{2} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{12}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence I could be a geometric sequence." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1cd1d0cb-5c67-54b2-9a8e-55d3e3199e6f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1cd1d0cb-5c67-54b2-9a8e-55d3e3199e6f" :answer-field/id #uuid "1cd1d0cb-5c67-54b2-9a8e-55d3e3199e6f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b5134393-8754-56f1-8c80-963cf9ae8285" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d89c9e75-1551-5bde-9f68-e97033024c24" "answer-b5134393-8754-56f1-8c80-963cf9ae8285" "answer-42dcbbf9-138e-544e-83b5-ce1af281813a" "answer-c8637f9e-b6c7-563c-8fbb-5358af318a7a" "answer-e7ee9576-7d5a-5cf5-bd8b-7b448a345983"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d89c9e75-1551-5bde-9f68-e97033024c24" :answer/id #uuid "d89c9e75-1551-5bde-9f68-e97033024c24" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b5134393-8754-56f1-8c80-963cf9ae8285" :answer/id #uuid "b5134393-8754-56f1-8c80-963cf9ae8285" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-42dcbbf9-138e-544e-83b5-ce1af281813a" :answer/id #uuid "42dcbbf9-138e-544e-83b5-ce1af281813a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c8637f9e-b6c7-563c-8fbb-5358af318a7a" :answer/id #uuid "c8637f9e-b6c7-563c-8fbb-5358af318a7a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e7ee9576-7d5a-5cf5-bd8b-7b448a345983" :answer/id #uuid "e7ee9576-7d5a-5cf5-bd8b-7b448a345983" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-011f3c60-0a40-5c48-8e42-7ae45f302869" :question/id #uuid "011f3c60-0a40-5c48-8e42-7ae45f302869" :question/math-academy-id "q-79509" :question/problem "Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

$$
1,\quad\:\: 3,\quad\:\: 9,\quad\:\: 27,\quad\:\: 81,\quad\:\: \ldots

Notice that each term is ${\color{blue}3}$ times the previous term:

![](images/9a/9a3af8dd763aa0ab6b176a3a9d711ead4d029e2cebef823f906403be5fc38786.png)

A sequence like the one above, where each term is found by multiplying the previous term by a fixed constant, is called a **geometric sequence**. 

This fixed constant is called the **common ratio**, and is denoted by $r.$ In this particular case, the common ratio is $r={\color{blue}3}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078694 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166765 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8198f6db-6c5f-5983-9cb0-0bd0190f9596" "question-2bf70c41-d3e4-5066-92f9-b0265e8edce1" "question-84e76c93-4252-53d8-b14a-d598aa6e8e08" "question-da5d7294-c739-5f77-ae4a-e6ad7eaa5e42" "question-d8788c2a-c953-5587-a4b0-071fdea7bf08"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166766 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-56abd260-e88d-5e15-85ad-d09d0617c5fa" "question-e713a272-c241-525b-b381-4fe5ba553286" "question-83895ad6-7f6a-50d5-a3b6-af8475bcabcc" "question-56f1a503-7979-5afa-a86c-36de0338e547"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-8198f6db-6c5f-5983-9cb0-0bd0190f9596" :question/id #uuid "8198f6db-6c5f-5983-9cb0-0bd0190f9596" :question/math-academy-id "q-341473" :question/problem "$$

If $y=\operatorname{arcsch}⁡({x}^{2}+4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4),$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+4}$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosecant function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,[\operatorname{arcsch}⁡({x}^{2}+4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{|{x}^{2}+4|\sqrt{1+{({x}^{2}+4)}^{2}}}\cdot {({x}^{2}+4)}^{′}-\frac{{({x}^{2}+4)}^{′}}{{x}^{2}+4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{({x}^{2}+4)\sqrt{1+({x}^{4}+8{x}^{2}+16)}}\cdot 2x-\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+4} \\  & =-\frac{2x}{({x}^{2}+4)\sqrt{{x}^{4}+8{x}^{2}+17}}-\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+4} \\  & =-\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+4}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{4}+8{x}^{2}+17}}+1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-520cf314-e244-5017-a78d-80675136c535"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-520cf314-e244-5017-a78d-80675136c535" :answer-field/id #uuid "520cf314-e244-5017-a78d-80675136c535" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-a0cd6cc1-2306-5ff5-bd40-675798a9d210" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a0cd6cc1-2306-5ff5-bd40-675798a9d210"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a0cd6cc1-2306-5ff5-bd40-675798a9d210" :answer/id #uuid "a0cd6cc1-2306-5ff5-bd40-675798a9d210" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{4}+8{x}^{2}+17}}+1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2bf70c41-d3e4-5066-92f9-b0265e8edce1" :question/id #uuid "2bf70c41-d3e4-5066-92f9-b0265e8edce1" :question/math-academy-id "q-95516" :question/problem "$$

If $y=\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(-2x),$ then $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosecant function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x)=-\frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get
