$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=8,\,{a}_{2}=6x,\,{a}_{3}=10x.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{6x}{8}=\frac{3x}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{10x}{6x}=\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x}{4} & =\frac{5}{3} \\ 3x & =\frac{20}{3} \\ x & =\frac{20}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5fd92fce-27a7-528b-8997-468fa342ecb8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5fd92fce-27a7-528b-8997-468fa342ecb8" :answer-field/id #uuid "5fd92fce-27a7-528b-8997-468fa342ecb8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1582d224-094e-567c-a4d0-6a766eb83c10" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8082c854-a0c3-5658-9917-19fdd468998e" "answer-1582d224-094e-567c-a4d0-6a766eb83c10" "answer-75fba1b8-0f25-52b0-a4e5-d85355af26f1" "answer-e86e41a3-1743-5eae-a35d-1b9bb6aa8392" "answer-3acc9f02-23f0-5267-8e8f-2d43767b5290"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8082c854-a0c3-5658-9917-19fdd468998e" :answer/id #uuid "8082c854-a0c3-5658-9917-19fdd468998e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{20}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1582d224-094e-567c-a4d0-6a766eb83c10" :answer/id #uuid "1582d224-094e-567c-a4d0-6a766eb83c10" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{20}{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-75fba1b8-0f25-52b0-a4e5-d85355af26f1" :answer/id #uuid "75fba1b8-0f25-52b0-a4e5-d85355af26f1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e86e41a3-1743-5eae-a35d-1b9bb6aa8392" :answer/id #uuid "e86e41a3-1743-5eae-a35d-1b9bb6aa8392" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{9}{20}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3acc9f02-23f0-5267-8e8f-2d43767b5290" :answer/id #uuid "3acc9f02-23f0-5267-8e8f-2d43767b5290" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5bf4971e-04f4-56ea-b8f7-ec174707b886" :question/id #uuid "5bf4971e-04f4-56ea-b8f7-ec174707b886" :question/math-academy-id "q-52474" :question/problem "Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $-1,\,-6,\,-36,\,…$

II. $1,\,-4,\,-16,\,…$

III. $2,\,7,\,12,\,…$" :question/worked-solution "A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-6)}{(-1)}=6 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-36)}{(-6)}=6\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-4)}{1}=-4 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-16)}{(-4)}=4\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is also not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{7}{2} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{12}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence I could be a geometric sequence." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1cd1d0cb-5c67-54b2-9a8e-55d3e3199e6f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1cd1d0cb-5c67-54b2-9a8e-55d3e3199e6f" :answer-field/id #uuid "1cd1d0cb-5c67-54b2-9a8e-55d3e3199e6f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b5134393-8754-56f1-8c80-963cf9ae8285" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d89c9e75-1551-5bde-9f68-e97033024c24" "answer-b5134393-8754-56f1-8c80-963cf9ae8285" "answer-42dcbbf9-138e-544e-83b5-ce1af281813a" "answer-c8637f9e-b6c7-563c-8fbb-5358af318a7a" "answer-e7ee9576-7d5a-5cf5-bd8b-7b448a345983"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d89c9e75-1551-5bde-9f68-e97033024c24" :answer/id #uuid "d89c9e75-1551-5bde-9f68-e97033024c24" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b5134393-8754-56f1-8c80-963cf9ae8285" :answer/id #uuid "b5134393-8754-56f1-8c80-963cf9ae8285" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-42dcbbf9-138e-544e-83b5-ce1af281813a" :answer/id #uuid "42dcbbf9-138e-544e-83b5-ce1af281813a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c8637f9e-b6c7-563c-8fbb-5358af318a7a" :answer/id #uuid "c8637f9e-b6c7-563c-8fbb-5358af318a7a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e7ee9576-7d5a-5cf5-bd8b-7b448a345983" :answer/id #uuid "e7ee9576-7d5a-5cf5-bd8b-7b448a345983" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-011f3c60-0a40-5c48-8e42-7ae45f302869" :question/id #uuid "011f3c60-0a40-5c48-8e42-7ae45f302869" :question/math-academy-id "q-79509" :question/problem "Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $120,\,80,\,30,\,…$

II. $-243,\,27,\,-3,\,…$

III. $225,\,45,\,9,\,…$" :question/worked-solution "A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{80}{120}=\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{30}{80}=\frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{27}{(-243)}=-\frac{1}{9} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-3)}{27}=-\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is also geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{45}{225}=\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{9}{45}=\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequences II and III could be geometric sequences." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2cef64b1-c161-50e4-82e1-fafe2dafb2db"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2cef64b1-c161-50e4-82e1-fafe2dafb2db" :answer-field/id #uuid "2cef64b1-c161-50e4-82e1-fafe2dafb2db" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4119ef5a-ce8f-557a-86d3-930060c2d7af" :answer-field/choices ["answer-466b273e-c846-58e4-b675-7fc925b9a67b" "answer-dd63c68f-2391-56cd-bd26-5b2e6bf05ebe" "answer-4119ef5a-ce8f-557a-86d3-930060c2d7af" "answer-d499038b-1ca3-508e-ade3-a293c9a995d0" "answer-d2daa668-266e-57f8-9b6d-9aba42612c84"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-466b273e-c846-58e4-b675-7fc925b9a67b" :answer/id #uuid "466b273e-c846-58e4-b675-7fc925b9a67b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dd63c68f-2391-56cd-bd26-5b2e6bf05ebe" :answer/id #uuid "dd63c68f-2391-56cd-bd26-5b2e6bf05ebe" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4119ef5a-ce8f-557a-86d3-930060c2d7af" :answer/id #uuid "4119ef5a-ce8f-557a-86d3-930060c2d7af" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d499038b-1ca3-508e-ade3-a293c9a995d0" :answer/id #uuid "d499038b-1ca3-508e-ade3-a293c9a995d0" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d2daa668-266e-57f8-9b6d-9aba42612c84" :answer/id #uuid "d2daa668-266e-57f8-9b6d-9aba42612c84" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079625 :tutorial/content "Consider the following sequence:

$$
1,\quad\:\: 3,\quad\:\: 9,\quad\:\: 27,\quad\:\: 81,\quad\:\: \ldots
$$

Notice that each term is ${\color{blue}3}$ times the previous term:

"$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]-81[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -24 \\ -24 & -72\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-I & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}72 & -24 \\ -24 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{27}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{9}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-92ef2ffd-6bce-5a3c-9878-3c95874f4572"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-92ef2ffd-6bce-5a3c-9878-3c95874f4572" :answer-field/id #uuid "92ef2ffd-6bce-5a3c-9878-3c95874f4572" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-dafadf4d-f436-5d63-ba00-63f2baf56d03" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2b2efb8c-2656-5a9e-bdf4-74177ad5bfa0" "answer-ada77caf-e98c-55fb-aefb-f3d728826900" "answer-e183294d-0160-5657-9a79-b2a38d4cd596" "answer-ab956e6c-1981-5cd4-973f-cb9d389db8f4" "answer-dafadf4d-f436-5d63-ba00-63f2baf56d03"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2b2efb8c-2656-5a9e-bdf4-74177ad5bfa0" :answer/id #uuid "2b2efb8c-2656-5a9e-bdf4-74177ad5bfa0" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]$

$x^3+x^2-9x-9=0.$" :question/worked-solution "We proceed to factor the left-hand side by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-9x-9 & = \\ ({x}^{3}+{x}^{2})-(9x+9) & = \\ {x}^{2}(x+1)-9(x+1) & = \\ (x+1)\cdot {x}^{2}-(x+1)\cdot 9 & = \\ (x+1)({x}^{2}-9) & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve $(x+1)(x^2-9) = 0$ by setting each factor equal to $0.$

- Setting the factor $(x+1)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =0 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Setting the factor $(x^2-9)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-1, \, \pm  3.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083246 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bb562da5-ef3b-592a-bfc0-4d26f88b1f50"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083042 :question/problem "Solve $2x^3+3x^2-8x-12=0.$" :question/worked-solution "We proceed to factor the left side by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-8x-12 & = \\ (2{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2})-(8x+12) & = \\ {x}^{2}(2x+3)-4(2x+3) & = \\ (2x+3)\cdot {x}^{2}-(2x+3)\cdot 4 & = \\ (2x+3)({x}^{2}-4)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve $(2x+3)(x^2-4) = 0$ by setting each factor equal to $0.$

- Setting the factor $(2x+3)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+3 & =0 \\ 2x & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Setting the factor $(x^2-4)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-2, \; -\dfrac{3}{2}, \; 2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083275 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bbddec8f-0415-5a7f-a473-3ac96a89f653"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083068 :question/problem "Solve $-x^3-4x^2+5x+20=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we multiply the equation by $-1$ to make the coefficient of the cubic term positive. This gives

$$
x^3+4x^2-5x-20=0.
$$

We then proceed to factor the left-hand side by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-5x-20 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}(x+4)-5(x+4) & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-5)(x+4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve $(x^2-5)(x+4)=0$ by setting each factor equal to $0.$

- Setting the factor $(x^2-5)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =5 \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Setting the factor $(x+4)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-4, \pm \sqrt 5.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083247 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-faa06da2-05be-56dd-9e44-883b8d4527f9" "question-f6abbc6d-e05c-5882-80a0-628ebefcab1b" "question-3e7651d9-4306-5281-ab2c-60e5fbcc4dde"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083043 :question/problem "Solve $8x^3+3=4x^2+6x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we subtract $4x^2$ and $6x$ from both sides to make the right side $0.$ To prepare for factoring by grouping, we make sure to write the resulting cubic in standard form.

$$
8x^3-4x^2-6x+3=0
$$

Next, we factor by grouping. Notice that when grouping the smaller terms, we factor out the negative sign.

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-6x+3 & = \\ (8{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2})-(6x-3) & = \\ 4{x}^{2}(2x-1)-3(2x-1) & = \\ (2x-1)\cdot 4{x}^{2}-(2x-1)\cdot 3 & = \\ (2x-1)(4{x}^{2}-3).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we set each factor equal to $0$ and solve.

- Setting the factor $(2x-1)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-1 & =0 \\ 2x & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Setting the factor $(4x^2-3)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-3 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2} & =3 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x= -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, \; \dfrac12, \; \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-e76e6bf7-d54d-5018-81b2-f60c46589b4a" :question/id #uuid "e76e6bf7-d54d-5018-81b2-f60c46589b4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-72088" :question/problem "Solve $y$ if ${y}^{3}+5{y}^{2}-2y-10=0.$" :question/worked-solution "We proceed to factor the left-hand side by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}+5{y}^{2}-2y-10 & = \\ ({y}^{3}+5{y}^{2})-(2y+10) & = \\ {y}^{2}(y+5)-2(y+5) & = \\ (y+5)\cdot {y}^{2}-(y+5)\cdot 2 & = \\ (y+5)({y}^{2}-2) & .\end{aligned}

"Given that $y=\sqrt{2x-1},$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=2x-1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7e463a5a-0bf7-5c15-8a84-e8fb513aab4c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-314192" :question/problem "The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{4x+1}$ at the point where $x=0$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=4x+1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}})|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(0)+1}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3b694189-fec1-5a06-8456-a524e215acf6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3b694189-fec1-5a06-8456-a524e215acf6" :answer-field/id #uuid "3b694189-fec1-5a06-8456-a524e215acf6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-33c7c493-bcdb-5703-aa16-7951eec23ed2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-33c7c493-bcdb-5703-aa16-7951eec23ed2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-33c7c493-bcdb-5703-aa16-7951eec23ed2" :answer/id #uuid "33c7c493-bcdb-5703-aa16-7951eec23ed2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-930f9486-b8c5-5ccf-b917-a4806acde6bf" :question/id #uuid "930f9486-b8c5-5ccf-b917-a4806acde6bf" :question/math-academy-id "q-314207" :question/problem "Given that $f(x)={({x}^{4}-3{x}^{3})}^{2},$ find ${f}^{′}(x).$

The graph above shows a direct variation between the variables $y$ and $x.$ Which equation describes the relationship between the variables?" :question/worked-solution "Since $y$ varies directly with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=kx.
$$

Next, we notice there is a point on the graph with $y=8$ and $x=2.$ So, we substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =k\cdot 2 \\ \frac{8}{2} & =k \\ 4 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

{:db/id 17592186362338 :question/worked-solution "We must find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=10.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=10
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨3,-1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}3=2\lambda x \\ -1=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{3}{2\lambda } \\ y=-\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=10$ and solve for $\lambda ,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{4{\lambda }^{2}}+\frac{1}{4{\lambda }^{2}} & =10 \\ \frac{10}{4{\lambda }^{2}} & =10 \\ 4{\lambda }^{2} & =1 \\ \lambda  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $x$ and $y.$ This gives

$$
x=\pm 3,\,y=∓1.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-3,1),\,(3,-1).

| $\,(x,y)\,$ | $\,(-3,1)\,$ | $\,(3,-1)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $\,-4\,$ | $\,16\,$ |

∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=0
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨8x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x=8\lambda x \\ 2y=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(1-4\lambda )=0 \\ y(1-\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8=0$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-8 & =0\,⇒\,y=\pm 2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,-2\sqrt{2}),(0,2\sqrt{2}).$

- Assuming $\lambda =\frac{1}{4}$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1-\frac{1}{4})=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the constraint condition $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8=0$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\pm \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(-\sqrt{2},0),(\sqrt{2},0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\pm \sqrt{2},0),\,(0,\pm 2\sqrt{2}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(\pm \sqrt{2},0)$ | $(0,\pm 2\sqrt{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $4$ | $10$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at the points $(\pm \sqrt{2},0)$ and its minimum value is $4.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281545 :question/worked-solution "We need to find the minimum value of $f$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y,z)={z}^{2}-xy-4=0.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at the points $(0,0,\pm 2),$ and its minimum value is $7.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281542 :question/worked-solution "We need to find the minimum value of $f$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y,z)=9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=36.$

\{\begin{aligned}x=9\lambda x \\ y=4\lambda y \\ z=\lambda z\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}(1-9\lambda )x=0 \\ (1-4\lambda )y=0 \\ (1-\lambda )z=0\end{aligned}

$$
9{x}^{2}=36\,⇒\,x=\pm 2.
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm 2,0,0).$

$$
4{y}^{2}=36\,⇒\,y=\pm 3.
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\pm 3,0).$

- Finally, assume that $\lambda =1.$ Then, by the first and second equations, we must have $x=y=0.$ Also, by the constraint $g(x,y,z)=36,$ we have

$$
{z}^{2}=36\,⇒\,z=\pm 6.
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,0,\pm 6).$

| $\,(x,y,z)\,$ | $\,(\pm 2,0,0)\,$ | $\,(0,\pm 3,0)\,$ | $\,(0,0,\pm 6)\,$ |

| $\,f(x,y,z)\,$ | $\,4\,$ | $\,9\,$ | $\,36\,$ |

$$

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at the points $(\pm 2,0,0),$ and its minimum value is $4.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186362343 :question/worked-solution "We need to find the maximum value of $f$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.$ 

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.

$$

$$

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2x=2\lambda x \\ -z=2\lambda y \\ -y=2\lambda z\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(\lambda -1)=0 \\ y(4{\lambda }^{2}-1)=0 \\ z=-2\lambda y\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- First, assume that $\lambda \ne 1$ and $\lambda \ne \pm \frac{1}{2}.$ Then, the solution of the above system is $x=y=z=0.$ But this contradicts the constraint $g(x,y,z)=1.$

- Next, assume that $\lambda =1.$ Then, by the second and third equations, we must have $y=z=0.$ Also, by the constraint $g(x,y,z)=1,$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}=1\,⇒\,x=\pm 1.
$$

This gives the critical point $(\pm 1,0,0).$

- Finally, assume that $\lambda =\pm \frac{1}{2}.$ Then, by the first and third equations, we must have $x=0$ and $z=∓y.$ Also, by the constraint $g(x,y,z)=1,$ we have

$$
{y}^{2}+(-y)^{2}=1\,⇒\,y=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

The corresponding values of $z$ are

$$
z=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}),(0,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}).$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $\,(x,y,z)\,$ | $\,(0,-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\,$ | $\,(0,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\,$ | $\,(\pm 1,0,0)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y,z)\,$ | $\,\pm \frac{1}{2}\,$ | $\,∓\frac{1}{2}\,$ | $\,1\,$ |

$$

$$

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at the points $(\pm 1,0,0),$  and its maximum value is $1.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186362344 :question/worked-solution "We need to find the maximum value of $f$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=35.$ 

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=35
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨2,6,10⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2=2\lambda x \\ 6=2\lambda y \\ 10=2\lambda z\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{\lambda } \\ y=\frac{3}{\lambda } \\ z=\frac{5}{\lambda }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x,\,y$ and $z$ into the condition $g(x,y,z)=35$ and solve for $\lambda ,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =35 \\ \frac{1}{{\lambda }^{2}}+\frac{9}{{\lambda }^{2}}+\frac{25}{{\lambda }^{2}} & =35 \\ \frac{35}{{\lambda }^{2}} & =35 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =1 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $x,\,y$ and $z.$ This gives

$$
x=\pm 1\,y=\pm 3\,z=\pm 5.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-1,-3,-5),\,(1,3,5).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $\,(x,y,z)\,$ | $\,(-1,-3,-5)\,$ | $\,(1,3,5)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y,z)\,$ | $\,-70\,$ | $\,70\,$ |

$$

$$

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(1,3,5),$ and its maximum value is $70.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]}] "assertions" [["knowledge-point-05b40dd4-a99b-5d5e-93b4-767ed99d62a0" :knowledge-point/id #uuid "05b40dd4-a99b-5d5e-93b4-767ed99d62a0"] [17592186408190 :topic/knowledge-points "knowledge-point-05b40dd4-a99b-5d5e-93b4-767ed99d62a0"] ["question-4ced75f7-e2c9-50f2-b2cf-114222fc960d" :question/id #uuid "4ced75f7-e2c9-50f2-b2cf-114222fc960d"] ["question-4ced75f7-e2c9-50f2-b2cf-114222fc960d" :question/math-academy-id "e-24942"] ["question-4ced75f7-e2c9-50f2-b2cf-114222fc960d" :question/problem "A scientist records how long it takes for a chemical reaction to complete. The experiment is conducted $40$ times. The table below shows the results.

a reaction completing in less than $20$ seconds."] ["question-4ced75f7-e2c9-50f2-b2cf-114222fc960d" :question/worked-solution "One event is more likely than another if it has a greater probability of occurring. If two events have the same probability, they are equally likely.

Let's consider each statement in turn.

- To compute the experimental probability of a reaction completing in more than $30$ seconds, we divide the number of times a reaction took more than $30$ seconds $(7+5=12)$ by the total number of trials $(40).$ This gives
![](images/41/41ae3b0ee5b77a5967ee949abfd5dc5327fc840e9061cecf1dfd52728405415f.svg)

This probability is a small number, closer to $0.$ Since

$$
0 < \dfrac{3}{10} < \dfrac12,
$$

this event is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{unlikely}}.$

- To compute the experimental probability of a reaction completing in less than $20$ seconds, we divide the number of times a reaction took less than $20$ seconds $(6+14=20)$ by the total number of trials $(40).$ This gives
![](images/19/194542c8095442fe631a733e681d43b025ac5b5f7f478f7b3c541e3c51718c69.svg)

Since the probability is $\dfrac12,$ this event is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{as likely as not}}.$

- The experimental probability of a reaction completing in more than $30$ seconds is less than the experimental probability of a reaction completing in less than $20$ seconds:

$$
\dfrac{3}{10} < \dfrac12.
$$

Therefore, a reaction completing in more than $30$ seconds is
$\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{less likely than}}$
a reaction completing in less than $20$ seconds."] ["knowledge-point-05b40dd4-a99b-5d5e-93b4-767ed99d62a0" :knowledge-point/canonical-example "question-4ced75f7-e2c9-50f2-b2cf-114222fc960d"] ["knowledge-point-05b40dd4-a99b-5d5e-93b4-767ed99d62a0" :knowledge-point/title "Comparing Two Events by Likelihood"] ["question-e4735ca8-e709-5697-8aaf-f9b52ab3104d" :question/id #uuid "e4735ca8-e709-5697-8aaf-f9b52ab3104d"] ["question-e4735ca8-e709-5697-8aaf-f9b52ab3104d" :question/math-academy-id "q-360663"] ["question-e4735ca8-e709-5697-8aaf-f9b52ab3104d" :question/problem "Sarah conducts an experiment $40$ times to see how quickly a machine sorts a bin of parts. The table below shows the results of her experiments.

| Time (seconds) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $<20$ | $6$ |
| $20-30$ | $16$ |
| $30-40$ | $10$ |

a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds."] ["question-e4735ca8-e709-5697-8aaf-f9b52ab3104d" :question/worked-solution "One event is more likely than another if it has a greater probability of occurring. If two events have the same probability, they are equally likely.

Let's consider each statement in turn.

- To compute the experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds, we divide the number of times a machine sorted a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds $(6+16=22)$ by the total number of times Sarah conducted the experiment $(40).$ This gives

$$
P(\text{sorts in }<30\text{ seconds})=\frac{22}{40}.
$$

This probability is a relatively large number, closer to $1.$ Since

$$
\frac{1}{2}<\frac{22}{40}<1,
$$

this event is $\text{likely}.$

- To compute the experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds, we divide the number of times a machine sorted a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds $(10+5+3=18)$ by the total number of times Sarah conducted the experiment $(40).$ This gives

$$
P(\text{sorts in }>30\text{ seconds})=\frac{18}{40}.
$$

This probability is a small number, closer to $0.$ Since

$$
0<\frac{18}{40}<\frac{1}{2},
$$

this event is $\text{unlikely}.$

- The experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds is *greater than* the experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds:

$$
P(\text{sorts in }<30\text{ seconds})=\frac{22}{40}>\frac{18}{40}=P(\text{sorts in }>30\text{ seconds})
$$

Therefore, a machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds is
$\text{more likely than}$
a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds."] ["question-e4735ca8-e709-5697-8aaf-f9b52ab3104d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] :question/problem "Given that $f(x)={x}^{2}$, the instantaneous rate of change ${f}^{′}(-1)$ can be computed using the limit of a difference quotient. The first few steps of this calculation are shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-1+h)-f(-1)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(-1+h)^{2}-(-1)^{2}}{h} \\  & =…\end{aligned}
$$

Finish the calculation, and hence find ${f}^{′}(-1).$"] ["question-7fa38cf7-46e9-5719-8fa2-6633394b103a" :question/worked-solution "By proceeding with the remaining calculations we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-1+h)-f(-1)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(-1+h)^{2}-(-1)^{2}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1-2h+{h}^{2}-1}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{h(-2+h)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(-2+h) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(-1)=-2.$"] ["question-7fa38cf7-46e9-5719-8fa2-6633394b103a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-26e0a8d8-3d22-5a55-a37b-cb46b000140b" :answer-field/id :question/problem "Find the instantaneous rate of change of $f(x)=5{x}^{2}$ at the point $x=1$ by computing the limit of a difference quotient."] ["question-01c94ce2-04ad-5708-8ba5-8bfca9809325" :question/worked-solution "*Method 1:*

By the definition, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(1)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}.
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=5{x}^{2}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{5(1+h)^{2}-5(1)^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{5+10h+5{h}^{2}-5}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{10h+5{h}^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(10+5h) \\  & =10+(0) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

 

*Method 2:*

By the definition, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(1)={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)-f(1)}{x-1}.
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=5{x}^{2}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1) & ={lim}_{x\to 1}(\frac{5{x}^{2}-5(1)^{2}}{x-1}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}(\frac{5({x}^{2}-1)}{x-1}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}(\frac{5(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}5(x+1) \\  & =5(1+1) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-01c94ce2-04ad-5708-8ba5-8bfca9809325" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-140d3701-ba23-5c26-9cf9-6d695b5d1f47" :answer-field/id #uuid the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)=\sqrt{x+y+4},$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=2+ax+\frac{1}{4}y-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{2}+bxy+c{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$"] ["question-f0b66b9d-4d88-5de4-a9f2-e4468c8b8ed2" :question/worked-solution "If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y+4}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y+4}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =\frac{1}{4}, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32} \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32} \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈2+\frac{1}{4}\cdot x+\frac{1}{4}\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{32}\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-\frac{1}{32})\cdot xy+(-\frac{1}{32})\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =2+\frac{1}{4}x+\frac{1}{4}y-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{2}+(-\frac{1}{32})xy+(-\frac{1}{64}){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=\frac{1}{4}+(-\frac{1}{32})+(-\frac{1}{64})=\frac{13}{64}.
$$"] ["question-f0b66b9d-4d88-5de4-a9f2-e4468c8b8ed2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-57708cab-0a02-5b87-93ec-6746644b7829" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x+{e}^{y}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{{e}^{y}}{x+{e}^{y}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =1, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\frac{{e}^{y}}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{x{e}^{y}}{(x+{e}^{y})^{2}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈0+1\cdot x+1\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-1)\cdot xy+0\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1x+1y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+(-1)xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1+1+(-1)=1.
$$"] ["question-983968fc-15f6-5756-ab92-7399b778fa93" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-be0946b1-502a-5aba-b006-539568a4bc82" :answer-field/id #uuid \textrm E\big[ X \,|\, Y = y \big] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, f_{X|Y}(x \,|\, y) \; \textrm{d}x.
$$

Note that $\textrm E\big[ X \,|\, Y = y \big]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{y-x}{\frac{1}{2}+y} \\  & =\frac{2(y-x)}{1+2y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $-1 \leq x \leq 0, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1.$ Outside this domain, we have $f_{X|Y} (x \,|\, y) = 0.$

Now, substituting $y=\dfrac{1}{2}$ into the expression for $f_{X|Y} (x \,|\, y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,\frac{1}{2}) & =\frac{2(\frac{1}{2}-x)}{1+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-2x}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"] [17592186161694 :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{2x+3}{6}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{1}^{2}(2{x}^{2}+3x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}((\frac{16}{3}+6)-(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{3}{2})) \\  & =\frac{55}{36}.\end{aligned}

Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1].$"] ["question-4aa42e03-e8d1-5333-8d07-d9074e34a91f" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(2-x-y)}{(\frac{3}{2}-y)} \\  & =\frac{4-2x-2y}{3-2y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{4-2x-2\cdot 1}{3-2\cdot 1}=\frac{4-2x-2}{3-2}=2-2x.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(2-2x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x-2{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-4aa42e03-e8d1-5333-8d07-d9074e34a91f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-8527a0b3-bf88-546e-9eb5-59cbca7c2a30" :answer-field/id #uuid \text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$

\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3x+{y}^{2}}{8})}{(\frac{3x+1}{8})} \\  & =\frac{3(x+{y}^{2})}{3x+1},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$

$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{3(1+{y}^{2})}{4}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4})-0] \\  & =\frac{9}{16}.\end{aligned}

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}}{24{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le y\le 4,\,0<x<\frac{1}{2}.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ for $0<y<1.$"] ["question-4c1f6156-411f-54e4-bb68-bbf84af25120" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{5})}{(\frac{6y+2}{5})} \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{6y+2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$ 

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \,\frac{6{x}^{2}+6y}{6y+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}+xy)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{2}y}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}[\frac{1}{4}+\frac{y}{2}-0] \\  & =\frac{6}{6y+2}\cdot \frac{1+2y}{4} \\  & =\frac{6}{2(3y+1)}\cdot \frac{(1+2y)}{4} \\  & =\frac{3(1+2y)}{4(3y+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-4c1f6156-411f-54e4-bb68-bbf84af25120" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-3d5798b6-1edf-5ed2-bbb7-aae35b6bf653" :answer-field/id #uuid random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the **conditional expectation of $X$ given $Y=y$** is defined as

$$
\textrm E[X |Y = y] =\int\limits_{\mathbb R} x \, f_{X|Y}(x|y)\;\textrm dx,
$$

where $f_{X|Y}(x|y)$ is the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y.$ 

This definition is similar to that of $\textrm{E}[X].$ However, we now use the conditional PDF $f_{X|Y}(x|y)$ instead of the marginal PDF $f_X(x)$ in our integral.

Note the following:

- When we select a particular value of $y,$ the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ returns a real number. However, if $y$ is not specified, i.e., $\textrm{E}[X |Y = y]$ *depends* on $y,$ we have that $\textrm{E}[X |Y = y]$ gives us a *function* of $y.$

- If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\textrm E[X | Y = y] = \textrm E[X]$ for all $y$.

- We sometimes use the notation $\mu_{X|y}$ to denote $E[X | Y = y].$

- We have an analogous definition for $\textrm E[Y |X = x]\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm E[Y |X = x] =\int\limits_{\mathbb R} y \, f_{Y|X}(y|x)\;\textrm dy,
$$

where $f_{Y|X}(y|x)$ is the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X.$"] [17592186163348 :tutorial/content "Let's find the conditional expectation $\textrm{E}\big[X \,|\, Y=1\big]$ given that the conditional probability density function $f_{X|Y}(x \,|\, 1)$ is given by

Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{″}(x)?$"] ["question-3aba7b06-41e0-5e22-b2ba-cc3cc44b0081" :question/worked-solution "First, if we denote $g(x)={f}^{′}(x)$ then ${f}^{″}(x)={g}^{′}(x).$ So, we need to sketch the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$ given the graph of $y=g(x),$ as usual.

Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=g(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${g}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $g(x)$ is increasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $g(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $g$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |
| ${g}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Additionally, the function $y=g(x)$ has inflection points at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5.$ At the inflection points, we have ${g}^{″}(x)=0,$ so the tangent to the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5.$ 

We don't know the exact values of ${g}^{′}(-0.5)$ and ${g}^{′}(0.5)$, but from the graph of $y=g(x)$ we find that the slope of the tangents to ${g}^{′}(x)$ at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5$ are positive and negative, respectively.

"step-2960f11d-8f32-50a8-8883-ed0e4c737260"] [17592186125083 :question/problem "Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1,$ and determine which of the following statements is true."] [17592186125083 :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2xy+3{y}^{2}+2x+10y+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2(x+y+1) & 2(x+3y+5)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+y+1=0 \\ x+3y+5=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
2y+4=0\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Then, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
x+(-2)+1=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Hence, $(1,-2)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2(x+3y+5))=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+y+1))=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2(x+3y+5))=6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,-2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,-2)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(1,-2),$ we get

$$
H(1,-2)=det({f}^{″}(1,-2))=2\cdot 6-{2}^{2}=8>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(1,-2)=({f}^{″}(1,-2))_{11}=2>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(1,-2).$"] [17592186125083 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}].
$$"] [17592186125084 :question/worked-solution "The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y & 3{y}^{2}-6x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-6y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}-6x.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6y=0 \\ 3{y}^{2}-6x=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
3{x}^{2}-6y=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})}^{2}-6x & =0 \\ \frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-2x & =0 \\ {x}^{4}-8x & =0 \\ x({x}^{3}-8) & =0 \\ x & =0,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y=\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
x=0\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}=0,\,\,x=2\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}=2.
$$

Hence, $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=6x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=-6 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-6y)=-6\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-6x)=6y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6x & -6 \\ -6 & 6y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))=0\cdot 0-(-6)^{2}=-36<0.
$$

Therefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(2,2),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(2,2)=[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 \\ -6 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(2,2),$ we get

$$
H(2,2)=det({f}^{″}(2,2))=12\cdot 12-(-6)^{2}=108>0.
$$

Finally, since $H(2,2)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(2,2)=({f}^{″}(2,2))_{11}=12>0,$ the function $f$ has a local minimum at $(2,2).$

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(2,2).$"] [17592186125084 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],
$$

and has a stationary point at $(3,-3).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $H(3,-3)>0$

II. $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)<0$

III. The point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum of $f$"] ["question-60652dd5-fdd9-5974-9d65-a71597afa3f3" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}4x+2y-6 & 2x+2y\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4x+2y-6,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+2y-6)=4 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+2y)=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(3,-3),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(3,-3)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(3,-3),$ we get

$$
H(3,-3)=det({f}^{″}(3,-3))=4\cdot 2-{2}^{2}=4>0.
$$

- Statement II is false. We have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)=({f}^{″}(3,-3))_{11}=4>0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(3,-3)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(3,-3)>0,$ the point $(3,-3)$ is a local minimum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""] ["question-60652dd5-fdd9-5974-9d65-a71597afa3f3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] - if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})=\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} & -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & -\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(-1,1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-1,1)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(-1,1),$ we get

$$
H(-1,1)=det({f}^{″}(-1,1))=(-2)^{2}-(-1)^{2}=3>0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)=({f}^{″}(-1,1))_{11}=-2<0.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(-1,1)>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(-1,1)<0,$ the point $(-1,1)$ is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

$$

$$

$$
\log\left(10^x\right) = x
$$

This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{3})-\operatorname{log}⁡(10t) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{3})-\operatorname{log}⁡(10\cdot 10) \\  & =2\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{3})-\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

The common logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=3$ and $x=2.$ Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{3})-\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{2})=2\cdot 3-2=4\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e5c7ea95-c351-53b5-8952-0f4a790122f8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-89a053ca-7dc5-596c-888f-925fbf0bae39" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-0714c123-409e-586b-bfd3-01ab5d4541d7"] [17592186084436 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the logarithm $\log (100).$ If no base is specified, then by default the base is equal to $10.$

In our example, we have

$$
\log(100)=\log_{10}(100)=\log_{10}(10^2) = 2.
$$

In general, the logarithm with base $10$ is called the **common logarithm**, and is defined as follows:

$a = 10^x$ is equivalent to $\log{a} = x$

Everything we did with logarithms, we can do with the common logarithm. For example, we can

- convert between exponential and logarithm form,

- evaluate common logarithm expressions, and

- calculate specific values of $\log a$ using a calculator.

Finally, note that most calculators have a button for the common logarithm. This is usually denoted $\log_{10}$ or simply $\log.$"] [17592186083421 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-e77b2e22-83c2-5884-b6a1-4a4bd43f7297" :question/id #uuid "e77b2e22-83c2-5884-b6a1-4a4bd43f7297"] ["question-e77b2e22-83c2-5884-b6a1-4a4bd43f7297" :question/math-academy-id "q-125854"] ["question-e77b2e22-83c2-5884-b6a1-4a4bd43f7297" :question/problem "$$

:question/problem "Using the definition of the hyperbolic cosine, calculate ${f}^{-1}(x)$ given that $f(x)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1)$ and $x\ge -1.$"] ["question-7e900458-4a34-53b2-8b6d-fd38c3b57268" :question/worked-solution "Let $y=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+1).$ Since $x\ge -1,$ we have $y\ge 1.$

To find the inverse function we swap $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
x=\operatorname{cosh}⁡(y+1),
$$

where $x\ge 1$ and $y\ge -1.$

Next, we apply the definition of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{y+1}+{e}^{-(y+1)}) \\ 2x & ={e}^{y+1}+{e}^{-(y+1)} \\ 2x{e}^{y+1} & ={e}^{2(y+1)}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Bringing everything to the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(y+1)}-2x{e}^{y+1}+1 & =0 \\ {({e}^{y+1})}^{2}-2x({e}^{y+1})+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $Y={e}^{y+1}.$ We can form a quadratic equation in $Y$ and solve it by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Y}^{2}-2xY+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2}-{x}^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (Y-x)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ Y-x & =\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ Y & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ {e}^{y+1} & =x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1} \\ y+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x\pm \sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Note that for  $x\ge 1,$ we have $x-\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\le 1$ and  $x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}\ge 1.$ Since $y+1\ge 0,$ the logarithm in the above equality must be non-negative. This requires its argument to be greater than or equal to $1$ for $x\ge 1$, so we reject the alternative with the negative sign. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1})-1.
$$"] ["question-7e900458-4a34-53b2-8b6d-fd38c3b57268" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-2a874508-e5a5-5caf-a21a-b4d69dce3efa" :answer-field/id #uuid Therefore, the $7$th term is $64.$"] [17592186078214 :question/problem "Given that $x$, $3x$, $36$ are the first three terms of a geometric sequence, find $x.$"] [17592186078214 :question/worked-solution "The first three terms are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=x,\,{a}_{2}=3x,\,{a}_{3}=36.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{3x}{x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{36}{3x}=\frac{12}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =\frac{12}{x} \\ 3x & =12 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186078201 :question/problem "Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{4}{2} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{8}{4} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}}=\frac{16}{8} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is also geometric. Again, for each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{(-\frac{1}{3})}{1} & =-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{(\frac{1}{9})}{(-\frac{1}{3})} & =-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}}=\frac{(-\frac{1}{27})}{(\frac{1}{9})} & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{8}{4} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{12}{8} & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequences I and II could be geometric sequences."] ["question-5d70384a-18d5-5ae8-aba3-5e0332c40c5f" :question/id #uuid "5d70384a-18d5-5ae8-aba3-5e0332c40c5f"] ["question-5d70384a-18d5-5ae8-aba3-5e0332c40c5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-250656"] ["question-5d70384a-18d5-5ae8-aba3-5e0332c40c5f" :question/problem "Consider the following geometric sequence:

\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=50,\,{a}_{2}=5x,\,{a}_{3}=12.5x.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{5x}{50}=\frac{x}{10}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{12.5x}{5x}=2.5.\end{aligned}

$$

three terms of a geometric sequence, find $x.$"] ["question-2e89be9b-05fd-570e-aab3-708af6042f1b" :question/worked-solution "The first three terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=8,\,{a}_{2}=6x,\,{a}_{3}=10x.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{6x}{8}=\frac{3x}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{10x}{6x}=\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$

:question/problem "Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

- Sequence I is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-6)}{(-1)}=6 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-36)}{(-6)}=6\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-4)}{1}=-4 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-16)}{(-4)}=4\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is also not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{7}{2} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{12}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence I could be a geometric sequence."] ["question-5bf4971e-04f4-56ea-b8f7-ec174707b886" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$

$$

- Sequence II is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$

$$

$$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-8198f6db-6c5f-5983-9cb0-0bd0190f9596" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosecant function is

$$

$$"] ["question-8198f6db-6c5f-5983-9cb0-0bd0190f9596" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-520cf314-e244-5017-a78d-80675136c535" :answer-field/id #uuid "520cf314-e244-5017-a78d-80675136c535"] ["answer-a0cd6cc1-2306-5ff5-bd40-675798a9d210" :answer/id #uuid "a0cd6cc1-2306-5ff5-bd40-675798a9d210"] ["answer-a0cd6cc1-2306-5ff5-bd40-675798a9d210" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-a0cd6cc1-2306-5ff5-bd40-675798a9d210" :answer/value "(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{4}+8{x}^{2}+17}}+1)"] ["answer-field-520cf314-e244-5017-a78d-80675136c535" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-520cf314-e244-5017-a78d-80675136c535" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-520cf314-e244-5017-a78d-80675136c535" :answer-field/correct "answer-a0cd6cc1-2306-5ff5-bd40-675798a9d210"] ["answer-field-520cf314-e244-5017-a78d-80675136c535" :answer-field/choices "answer-a0cd6cc1-2306-5ff5-bd40-675798a9d210"] ["question-8198f6db-6c5f-5983-9cb0-0bd0190f9596" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-520cf314-e244-5017-a78d-80675136c535"] [17592186166765 :knowledge-point/questions "question-8198f6db-6c5f-5983-9cb0-0bd0190f9596"] ["question-2bf70c41-d3e4-5066-92f9-b0265e8edce1" :question/id #uuid "2bf70c41-d3e4-5066-92f9-b0265e8edce1"] ["question-2bf70c41-d3e4-5066-92f9-b0265e8edce1" :question/math-academy-id "q-95516"] ["question-2bf70c41-d3e4-5066-92f9-b0265e8edce1" :question/problem "$$

Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$"] ["question-eeba80ad-bee9-5269-baef-fbd3bd2d6cda" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 3 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-81I & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]-81[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -24 \\ -24 & -72\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-81I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-I & =[\begin{aligned}73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}72 & -24 \\ -24 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{27}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{9}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-eeba80ad-bee9-5269-baef-fbd3bd2d6cda" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-92ef2ffd-6bce-5a3c-9878-3c95874f4572" :answer-field/id #uuid "92ef2ffd-6bce-5a3c-9878-3c95874f4572"] ["answer-2b2efb8c-2656-5a9e-bdf4-74177ad5bfa0" :answer/id #uuid "2b2efb8c-2656-5a9e-bdf4-74177ad5bfa0"] ["answer-2b2efb8c-2656-5a9e-bdf4-74177ad5bfa0" :answer/type :answer.type/text] ["answer-2b2efb8c-2656-5a9e-bdf4-74177ad5bfa0" :answer/value "$U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Next, we factor by grouping. Notice that when grouping the smaller terms, we factor out the negative sign.

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-6x+3 & = \\ (8{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2})-(6x-3) & = \\ 4{x}^{2}(2x-1)-3(2x-1) & = \\ (2x-1)\cdot 4{x}^{2}-(2x-1)\cdot 3 & = \\ (2x-1)(4{x}^{2}-3).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we set each factor equal to $0$ and solve.

- Setting the factor $(2x-1)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-1 & =0 \\ 2x & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Setting the factor $(4x^2-3)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-3 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2} & =3 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}+5{y}^{2}-2y-10 & = \\ ({y}^{3}+5{y}^{2})-(2y+10) & = \\ {y}^{2}(y+5)-2(y+5) & = \\ (y+5)\cdot {y}^{2}-(y+5)\cdot 2 & = \\ (y+5)({y}^{2}-2) & .\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-2 & =0 \\ {y}^{2} & =2 \\ y & =\pm \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}^{2}-6 & =0 \\ {b}^{2} & =6 \\ b & =\pm \sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}+3x-15 & = \\ ({x}^{3}-5{x}^{2})+(3x-15) & = \\ {x}^{2}(x-5)+3(x-5) & = \\ (x-5)\cdot {x}^{2}+(x-5)\cdot 3 & = \\ (x-5)({x}^{2}+3) & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve $(x-5)({x}^{2}+3)=0$ by setting each factor equal to $0.$

- Setting the factor $(x-5)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =0 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

- Setting the factor $({x}^{2}+3)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}^{2}+3) & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since a squared real number cannot be negative, the equation ${x}^{2}+3=0$ has no real solutions.

Therefore,  $x=5$ is the only real solution."] ["question-2a147b6b-b927-5c0b-b768-701655ad01fc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-6d8ec166-959b-5586-85f7-387a034ebd24" ["question-f6abbc6d-e05c-5882-80a0-628ebefcab1b" :question/worked-solution "Since we have an overall common factor of $5$, we start by dividing our equation through by $5.$ This gives 

$$
6{n}^{3}+3{n}^{2}-4n-2=0.
$$

Next, we factor by grouping. Notice that when grouping the smaller terms, we factor out the negative sign.

$$
\begin{aligned}6{n}^{3}+3{n}^{2}-4n-2 & = \\ (6{n}^{3}+3{n}^{2})-(4n+2) & = \\ 3{n}^{2}(2n+1)-2(2n+1) & = \\ (2n+1)\cdot 3{n}^{2}-(2n+1)\cdot 2 & = \\ (2n+1)(3{n}^{2}-2) & .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we set each factor equal to $0$ and solve:

- Setting the factor $(2n+1)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2n+1 & =0 \\ n & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Setting the factor $(3{n}^{2}-2)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{n}^{2}-2 & =0 \\ 3{n}^{2} & =2 \\ n & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the solutions to the given equation are $-\frac{1}{2}$ and $\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}.$"] ["question-f6abbc6d-e05c-5882-80a0-628ebefcab1b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["question-3e7651d9-4306-5281-ab2c-60e5fbcc4dde" :question/worked-solution "Since we have an overall common factor of $3$, we start by dividing our equation through by $3.$ This gives 

$$
{t}^{3}-5{t}^{2}-3t+15=0.
$$

Next, we factor by grouping. Notice that when grouping the smaller terms, we factor out the negative sign.

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3}-5{t}^{2}-3t+15 & = \\ ({t}^{3}-5{t}^{2})-(3t-15) & = \\ {t}^{2}(t-5)-3(t-5) & = \\ (t-5)\cdot {t}^{2}-(t-5)\cdot 3 & = \\ (t-5)({t}^{2}-3) & .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we set each factor equal to $0$ and solve:

- Setting the factor $(t-5)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}t-5 & =0 \\ t & =5\end{aligned}
$$

- Setting the factor $({t}^{2}-3)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-3 & =0 \\ {t}^{2} & =3 \\ t & =\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =2({g}^{-1/2})^{′}=-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}{g}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{{g}^{3/2}}, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{3}-2x)^{′}=3{x}^{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{g}^{3/2}}\cdot (3{x}^{2}-2) \\  & =-\frac{3{x}^{2}-2}{{g}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{3{x}^{2}-2}{\sqrt{({x}^{3}-2x)^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-321f22b7-0ca5-594c-82a7-c5cf5cf23fad" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-686cff4f-8265-5ba3-8560-bcdf5671d8d5" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Given that $y=\sqrt{2x-1},$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$"] ["question-98cde390-f268-5ffd-9f2f-31f016a0c432" :question/worked-solution "We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=2x-1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-98cde390-f268-5ffd-9f2f-31f016a0c432" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-7e463a5a-0bf7-5c15-8a84-e8fb513aab4c" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{4x+1}$ at the point where $x=0$ is{{field-1}}."] ["question-fa666076-05a3-50c7-be3d-b7a39d6d4f55" :question/worked-solution "To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=4x+1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}})|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(0)+1}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
y=4x.

To compute the constant of proportionality, we first need to choose a point $(x,y)$ on the graph. Here, let's choose the point $(3,1).$

![](images/be/bec01f9dc01b340075f09dd459571fe8199116f18a6ab912eb958c7a6f9ee4f2.png)

$$
k=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

Therefore, the equation is

$$
y=\frac{1}{3}x.
$$"] ["question-817c5709-21ea-5c46-9e06-c595f5917c73" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-df70821b-247b-5776-8c45-aa8d80611751" :answer-field/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Calculate ${log}_{8}⁡(32)$ without using a calculator." :question/worked-solution "We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}⁡X=\frac{{log}_{b}⁡X}{{log}_{b}⁡a}
$$

In our case, $a=8,$ and $X=32.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ are powers of $2,$ we set $b=2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}⁡(32) & =\frac{{log}_{2}⁡(32)}{{log}_{2}⁡(8)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{5})}{{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{3})} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049053} {:db/id 17592186048861 :topic/id #uuid "c70c51db-61f6-5d14-a3c6-bbee2caa27c6" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186054730 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id $$

$$
z = 0 + \sqrt{2} \textrm{i}
$$

We know that for a complex number

$$
z=a+b\textrm{i}
$$

the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
\mid z \mid = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}
$$

So, its magnitude of

$$
z=0 + \sqrt{2} \textrm{i}
$$

is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mid z \mid &= \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{(0)^{2} + (\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{0 + 2} \\
&= \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186055468 :question/id #uuid "31e8b641-430e-52d0-ad50-771deb4c09fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-70255"} {:db/id 17592186055469 :question/id #uuid "569dfd3a-4f17-5dc7-a6b5-3a7f2085a702" :question/math-academy-id "q-70257"} {:db/id 17592186515596 :question/id #uuid "c3ed3524-1800-5472-a34a-a2b28ed462d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-160277" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "008a9322-bc09-5270-b395-42f5ae02f992" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186514873} {:answer/id #uuid "2370feff-0720-50c4-8b43-d0d1aab5431b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186514956} {:answer/id #uuid "8ef6c697-69ee-5d21-b15c-a353586495fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186515175} {:answer/id #uuid "ab0f6764-317d-5061-9f80-de4f98c14068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186515231} {:answer/id #uuid "eb76ce3d-4469-58f1-ae4b-06566734b7f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186515369}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186515231} :answer-field/id #uuid "35aa10d9-d0b5-5bf2-a319-9f587b8c0a83" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186515429}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "What is the magnitude of the number $z=2\text{i}?$" :question/worked-solution "The imaginary number $2\text{i}$ is equivalent to the complex number $z=0+2\text{i}.$
