17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt[4]{e})=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite $\sqrt[4]{e}$ as a power of $e$ (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows:

$$
\sqrt[4]{e}={e}^{1/4}
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt[4]{e})=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{1/4})
$$

The natural logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{1/4})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186512917 :question/id #uuid "a5359436-369e-5935-88c6-73a8053a9364" :question/math-academy-id "q-66526" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186087692 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "169ca81a-c698-553c-9f47-d6c4303b82a9" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Natural Logarithms of Fractions and Roots"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6042c78b-71af-5276-80cf-ccdcb9284bf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186512329} {:answer/id #uuid "6614a67a-a7fe-55e2-be74-7e1ab3c9e3c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186512343} {:answer/id #uuid "b10534f0-4c95-531e-94d6-ba5e4a60964c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186512516} {:answer/id #uuid "c6fff638-a832-599c-b20d-b7725b1e8582" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186512578} {:answer/id #uuid "f7b61c9c-6858-5b2e-a66c-1ae788e691c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186512699}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "6614a67a-a7fe-55e2-be74-7e1ab3c9e3c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186512343} :answer-field/id #uuid "6fd07e78-dd69-5881-8015-dd32bee64dd0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186512789}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}})=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite $\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}$ as a power of $e$ (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows:

$$

Therefore, we have:

$$

17592186087581 :question/id #uuid "1e79a137-05cd-5dd5-bb0a-04c9040c05e4" :question/math-academy-id "e-5881" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186087854 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "18823139-c8c2-56ad-b8cc-4e43b97e904d" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Value of the Remainder When a Polynomial is Divided by a Linear Factor"}] :question/problem "Find the remainder when $p(x)=3x^2 +7x - 4$ is divided by $(3x-2)$." :question/worked-solution "The remainder theorem states that when $p(x)$ is divided by

$$
(3x-2)= 3\left(x-\dfrac23\right)
$$

the remainder equals

$$
p\left(\dfrac23\right)
$$

Evaluating

$$
p\left(\dfrac23\right)
$$

directly gives

$$
\begin{aligned} p\left(\dfrac23\right) & =3\cdot \left(\dfrac23\right)^2 +7\cdot \left(\dfrac23\right) - 4 \\[5pt] & =3\cdot \left(\dfrac49\right) +\dfrac{14}{3} - 4 \\[5pt] & =\dfrac{12}{9}+\dfrac{2}{3} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{12+ 3\cdot 2}{9} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{18}{9} \\[5pt] & = 2. \end{aligned}
$$

So, when $p(x)$ is divided by

$$
3\left(x-\dfrac23\right)
$$

the remainder is $2$.

**Note:** We can check the answer by carrying out synthetic division:

|  | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\color{red}\frac23$ | $3$ | $7$ | $\!\!\!\!-4$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $2$ | $6$ |
|  | $3$ | $9$ | $2$ |"} {:db/id 17592186087981 :question/id #uuid "6687eac2-7313-51d7-bcb7-c1db126988a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-112672"} {:db/id 17592186088156 :question/id #uuid "3b384836-65f4-5558-99cf-508f98f25e0e" :question/math-academy-id "q-38075"} {:db/id 17592186088327 :question/id #uuid "455e8957-17d6-5f95-a8b8-fa7a34d4b4bf" :question/math-academy-id "q-7622"} {:db/id 17592186087855 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186087582 :question/id #uuid "488cb495-bf1e-5f52-87a5-8bfc6fbbce16" :question/math-academy-id "e-5882"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c0dab780-3669-5234-8c5b-4b7f844f3a8f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186088158 :question/id #uuid "45ff9d10-2870-5ac8-aaa5-05260b910508" :question/math-academy-id "q-38201"} {:db/id 17592186088330 :question/id #uuid "02d3ff84-6fee-5006-bcc9-dc26c7c12a1e" :question/math-academy-id "q-7629"} {:db/id 17592186088335 :question/id #uuid "6949aebe-15da-5aae-8ed2-843a8ccfb512" :question/math-academy-id "q-7651"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Value of a Single Unknown in a Polynomial Given a Remainder"} {:db/id 17592186087582 :question/id #uuid "488cb495-bf1e-5f52-87a5-8bfc6fbbce16" :question/math-academy-id "e-5882" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186087855 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c0dab780-3669-5234-8c5b-4b7f844f3a8f" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Value of a Single Unknown in a Polynomial Given a Remainder"}] :question/problem "If $q(x)=2x^3+3x^2-5x+c$ has remainder $-5$ when divided by $(x+3)$, what is the value of $c$?" :question/worked-solution "The remainder theorem states that when $q(x)$ is divided by $(x+3)$, the remainder equals $q(-3)$. Since we're told that the remainder is $-5$, then, we must have $q(-3)=-5$.

Evaluating $q(-3)$ directly gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
q(-3) &= 2(-3)^{3} + 3(-3)^{2} - 5(-3) + c \\
&=-54 + 27 + 15 + c \\
&=-12 + c
\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
-5 = -12 + c
$$

Solving for $c$ in the equation above, we find that $c=7$."} {:db/id 17592186088158 :question/id #uuid "45ff9d10-2870-5ac8-aaa5-05260b910508" :question/math-academy-id "q-38201"} {:db/id 17592186088330 :question/id #uuid "02d3ff84-6fee-5006-bcc9-dc26c7c12a1e" :question/math-academy-id "q-7629"} {:db/id 17592186088335 :question/id #uuid "6949aebe-15da-5aae-8ed2-843a8ccfb512" :question/math-academy-id "q-7651"} {:db/id 17592186087856 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186087583 :question/id #uuid "6bbc5788-0449-51cb-815a-83f578ef6b15" :question/math-academy-id "e-5883"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ed971935-4ef9-5c49-a67d-26dde1a350bc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049060}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186088060 :question/id #uuid "221bd19a-a83b-59df-bca7-ed208e3d6846" :question/math-academy-id "q-18146"} {:db/id 17592186088063 :question/id #uuid "a23c5dd7-ef0f-5c2e-9745-956b0c0092d8" :question/math-academy-id "q-18935"} {:db/id 17592186512889 :question/id #uuid "5db961df-fac4-59ee-a59e-6595583c0931" :question/math-academy-id "q-112756"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Values of Two Unknowns in a Polynomial Given Two Remainders"} {:db/id 17592186087583 :question/id #uuid "6bbc5788-0449-51cb-815a-83f578ef6b15" :question/math-academy-id "e-5883" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186087856 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ed971935-4ef9-5c49-a67d-26dde1a350bc" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Values of Two Unknowns in a Polynomial Given Two Remainders"}] :question/problem "Suppose $f(x) = ax^3 +bx^2 -11x -2$ has a factor of $(x-2)$ and remainder of $-8$ when divided by $(x-1)$. Find the values of $a$ and $b$." :question/worked-solution "Since $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x)$, it must divide into $f(x)$ with no remainder. In other words, when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-2)$, the remainder is $0$. It follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 &= f(2) \\
&= a(2)^{3} + b(2)^{2} - 11(2) - 2 \\
&= 8a + 4b - 24
\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, since we're told that the remainder is $-8$ when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-1)$, it follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}
-8 &= f(1) \\
&= a(1)^{3} + b(1)^{2} - 11(1) - 2 \\
&= a + b - 13
\end{aligned}

value of $a-b.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $(x-1)$ is a factor of $f(x)$, it must divide into $f(x)$ with no remainder. In other words, when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-1),$ the remainder is $0.$ It follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =f(1) \\  & =a(1)^{3}-2(1)^{2}+b(1)+1 \\  & =a-2+b+1 \\  & =a+b-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, since we're told that the remainder is $4$ when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+2),$ it follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =f(-2) \\  & =a(-2)^{3}-2(-2)^{2}+b(-2)+1 \\  & =-8a-8-2b+1 \\  & =-8a-2b-7.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have the system of equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0=a+b-1 \\ 4=-8a-2b-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying each equation, we get

$$
\{\begin{aligned}a+b=1 \\ 8a+2b=-11.\end{aligned}
$$

To eliminate $b,$ we multiply the first equation by $-2,$ and we add the resulting equation to the second equation. So we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & -2a-2b=-2 \\ +\,\,\, & \,8a+2b=-11 \\  & \,6a=-13.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get $a=-\frac{13}{6}.$ Finally, we substitute it into $a+b=1$ to find $b=\frac{19}{6}.$ 

Therefore, our final solution is $a-b=-\frac{16}{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186049755 :topic/difficulty 0.7319924602535156 :topic/id #uuid "1125135d-4341-5e5d-9065-381cc0460203" :topic/knowledge-points :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186092327 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4eab94cb-5a5a-5915-ab95-963cb4c63817" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Closure Properties of Polynomials"}] :question/problem "Which of the following expressions are polynomials?

I. $(5x^2-10x^3) \div (5x)$

II. $(1-x^3) \div (x^3)$

III. $(2x^5) \cdot (-x^3-7)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that polynomials have the following closure properties:

- Polynomials are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication. This means that the sum, difference, and product of two polynomials is *always* a polynomial.

- Polynomials are *not* closed under division. This means that the quotient of two polynomials is *not* always a polynomial.

With that in mind, let's examine our expressions in turn.

- Expression I is a polynomial. Even though polynomials are *not* closed under division, the quotient of these two polynomials results in a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3})÷(5x) & =\frac{5{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3}}{5x} \\  & =\frac{5x(x-2{x}^{2})}{5x} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{5x}(x-2{x}^{2})}{\cancel{5x}} \\  & =x-2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Expression II is *not* a polynomial. Carrying out the division, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}-1\end{aligned}
$$

which is *not* a polynomial.

- Expression III is a polynomial. It's a product of two polynomials, and polynomials are closed under multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186048180} {:db/id 17592186048957} {:db/id 17592186049500} {:db/id 17592186050323} {:db/id 17592186092553 :question/id #uuid - Statement II is false. For example, suppose that $P=x^5$ and $Q=-x^5.$ Then $P+Q = x^5+(-x^5)=0,$ which is not a polynomial of degree $5.$

- Statement III is true. For example, suppose that $P=x^5$ and $Q=x^5.$ Then $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{x^5}{x^5} = 1,$ which is a polynomial of degree $0.$

2x^3 - 2x$ at the point $(1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x) = 2x^3 - 2x.$ Computing the derivative $f'(x)$ gives

$$
f'(x)  = 6x^2-2.
$$

We then compute $f'(1)$, which gives

$$
f'(1)  = 6(1)^2-2 = 4.
$$

a Tangent Line Intersects an Axis"}] :question/problem "Find where the tangent to the curve $y=4\sqrt{x}+4x$ at the point $(1,8)$ intersects the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)=4\sqrt{x}+4x.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\sqrt{x}+4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{1/2}+4x) \\  & =2{x}^{-1/2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
m=f'(1) = 2(1)^{-1/2}+4 = 6.
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-8 & =6(x-1) \\ y & =6x-6+8 \\ y & =6x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6x+2 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $\left(-\dfrac 1 3, 0\right).$"} {:db/id 17592186049394} {:db/id 17592186092504 :question/id #uuid "9bc53eba-4d4e-5f8c-8a22-7a4a98405447" Consider the picture shown above. Find a unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf a$." :question/worked-solution "![](images/b3/b316448c885a20a7ed60871ce0f1a4dc4f77bd4658dc6eda3407fb3c89a088cb.png)

In $\bigtriangleup AHB$ we have

$$
\angle AHB = 90^\circ
$$

, $AH=3$ and $BH=2$. So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
AB &= \sqrt{AH^{2} + BH^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{3^{2} + 2^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{9 + 4} \\
&= \sqrt{13}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $\mathbf{a}$ is $\sqrt{13}$. Consequently, the unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= \frac{1}{\mid a \mid} \cdot a \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}a
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049923} {:db/id 17592186050315} {:db/id 17592186502429} {:db/id 17592186097161 :question/id #uuid "9d05ca0e-131b-5294-8367-1760396e4369" :question/math-academy-id "q-19276"} ![](images/87/87647211f77776c5f5f740c205fafb150eef1b9d3ebefb82df73a9fdcd953bdb.png)

In $△AHB$, we have $∠AHB={90}^{∘}$, $AH=0.5=\frac{1}{2}$ and $BH=2.$ So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}|m+n| & =AB \\  & =\sqrt{A{H}^{2}+B{H}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+4} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $m+n$ is $\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.$ Consequently, the unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{1}{|m+n|}\cdot (m+n) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}(m+n).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502334 :question/id #uuid "15405bfd-218a-5ebb-ac44-be3eba615aca"} {:db/id 17592186502340 :question/id #uuid "25059bd6-40b8-5009-96b3-70ae023f7607"} {:db/id 17592186502342 Vector Parallel to a Vector Sum"}] :question/problem "The vector $\mathbf{a}$ is directed horizontally to the right and has magnitude $10$, while the vector $\mathbf{b}$ is directed vertically down and has magnitude $20$. Find a unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{a+b}$." :question/worked-solution "First, we have to find $\mathbf{a+b}$. According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}$ goes from the tail of $\mathbf{a}$ to the head of $\mathbf{b}$:

![](images/32/32c48d8c19fc68fbc172b240ded922f3e2ebc12804411c318ff63fe999aaedcc.png)

To find the unit vector corresponding to $\mathbf{a+b}$, we have to divide by the magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= \frac{a + b}{\mid a + b \mid}
\end{aligned}
$$

To find the magnitude, first notice that we obtain a right triangle. So, we can use the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{vmatrix}a + b & ^{2} &= & a & ^{2} +\left.\end{vmatrix}b\right|^{2} \\
&= 10^{2} + 20^{2} \\
&= 100 + 400 \\
&= 500
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mid \mathbf{a+b} &= \sqrt{500}=10\sqrt{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

and the corresponding unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= \frac{a + b}{\mid a + b \mid} \\
&= \frac{1}{10\sqrt{5}}(a + b)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186502535} {:db/id 17592186097042 :question/id #uuid "3f0752f9-cfba-5496-a6dc-d603b64b1e81" :question/math-academy-id "q-12184"} {:db/id 17592186097043 :question/id #uuid :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Product Rule to Compute a Limit Given a Graph"}] :question/problem "Find $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2}\left(\dfrac{x^3 f(x)}{4}\right)$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted below.

![](images/f4/f41914a12cf2ce0ec4799c4e9bacc3347e133f99747512a2211428e3571c4677.png)" :question/worked-solution "From the graph, we get that

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2} f(x)=4
$$

So, applying the product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 2)((x^{3}f(x))/(4)) &= \frac{1}{4} \cdot lim_(x → 2)x^{3} \cdot lim_(x → 2)f(x) \\
&= \frac{1}{4} \cdot 2^{3} \cdot 4 \\
&= 8
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186101387 :question/id #uuid "3f0c2ba6-4cc9-5ec3-b760-d0b989ee0f0b" :question/math-academy-id "q-35441"} {:db/id 17592186101388 :question/id #uuid "74d6c8be-493b-5971-9281-db18489c7367" :question/math-academy-id "q-35443"} {:db/id 17592186100824 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100659 :question/id #uuid "7a24a8e0-768e-541c-aff1-cad6f977da87" :question/math-academy-id "e-3562"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5feb914d-efad-5d89-85a9-db99befc9928" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050653}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101385 :question/id #uuid "2c5cae0e-9fc0-5479-96b3-13c68727e31a" :question/math-academy-id "q-35182"} {:db/id 17592186101386 :question/id #uuid "61336731-c818-58a0-bf90-6c02005e9762" :question/math-academy-id "q-35402"} {:db/id 17592186233420 :question/id #uuid "a350247e-7ecd-5d52-833a-6128b4df7d84" :question/math-academy-id "q-133327"} {:db/id 17592186235427 :question/id #uuid "4245aadd-c6cc-525e-9e00-1a2a6ed2d782" :question/math-academy-id "q-166293"}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Product Rule to Compute a Limit"} {:db/id 17592186100659 :question/id #uuid "7a24a8e0-768e-541c-aff1-cad6f977da87" :question/math-academy-id "e-3562" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186100824 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5feb914d-efad-5d89-85a9-db99befc9928" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Product Rule to Compute a Limit"}] :question/problem "Find $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow -2}(x^2-3x)(x+1)^{3}$." :question/worked-solution "Applying the product rule, followed by the sum and constant multiple rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → - 2)(x^{2} - 3x)(x + 1)^{3} &= lim_(x → - 2)(x^{2} - 3x) \cdot lim_(x → - 2)(x + 1)^{3} \\
&= (lim_(x → - 2)x^{2} - 3lim_(x → - 2)x)(lim_(x → - 2)(x^{3} + 3x^{2} + 3x + 1)) \\
&= ((-2)^{2} - 3(-2))((-2)^{3} + 3(-2)^{2} + 3(-2) + 1) \\
&= (4 + 6)(-8 + 12 - 6 + 1) \\
&= (10)(-1) \\
&=-10
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050653} {:db/id 17592186101385 :question/id #uuid "2c5cae0e-9fc0-5479-96b3-13c68727e31a" :question/math-academy-id "q-35182"} {:db/id 17592186101386 :question/id #uuid "61336731-c818-58a0-bf90-6c02005e9762" :question/math-academy-id "q-35402"} {:db/id 17592186233420 :question/id #uuid "a350247e-7ecd-5d52-833a-6128b4df7d84" :question/math-academy-id "q-133327"} {:db/id 17592186235427 :question/id #uuid "4245aadd-c6cc-525e-9e00-1a2a6ed2d782" :question/math-academy-id "q-166293"} {:db/id 17592186100952 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100620 :question/id #uuid "04538f07-6e4c-547e-be0c-8b62025e19ff" :question/math-academy-id "e-28"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0a649e49-73c7-5470-8361-2002da74f234" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101389 :question/id #uuid "82d65e26-7392-5b3a-8610-dcf039f7634a" :question/math-academy-id "q-35465"} {:db/id 17592186101419 :question/id #uuid "865eccb3-32c8-5bdb-8525-1edbac8859a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-4454"} {:db/id 17592186235468 :question/id #uuid "8205e6dc-0e96-51c9-b282-25c73bfff5de" :question/math-academy-id "q-167691"}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Quotient Rule to Compute a Limit"} {:db/id 17592186100620 :question/id #uuid "04538f07-6e4c-547e-be0c-8b62025e19ff" :question/math-academy-id "e-28" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186100952 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0a649e49-73c7-5470-8361-2002da74f234" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Quotient Rule to Compute a Limit"}] :question/problem "Calculate $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2} x^{-5}$." :question/worked-solution "First, we will express the negative exponent as a quotient:

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2} x^{-5}= \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2} \dfrac{1}{x^5}
$$

Then, we apply the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 2)x^{-5} &= (lim_(x → 2)1)/(lim_(x → 2)x^{5}) \\
&= \frac{1}{2^{5}} \\
&= \frac{1}{32}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186101389 :question/id #uuid "82d65e26-7392-5b3a-8610-dcf039f7634a" :question/math-academy-id "q-35465"} {:db/id 17592186101419 :question/id #uuid "865eccb3-32c8-5bdb-8525-1edbac8859a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-4454"} {:db/id 17592186235468 :question/id #uuid "8205e6dc-0e96-51c9-b282-25c73bfff5de" :question/math-academy-id "q-167691"} {:db/id 17592186100953 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100621 :question/id #uuid "71b3f83c-33e6-5043-9215-7db7b4b12497" :question/math-academy-id "e-29"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b0159149-010c-5bef-a28d-85c4c43f0586" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101241 :question/id #uuid "567477b4-0e84-5ce6-8417-768895c7e8ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-17281"} {:db/id 17592186101242 :question/id #uuid "8ac5ec7e-4a80-5557-9f6e-738dc68dcc67" :question/math-academy-id "q-17283"} {:db/id 17592186235507 :question/id #uuid "b9b71e21-f784-5d34-aeb2-f3980a06a6a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-167994"} {:db/id 17592186512873 :question/id #uuid "124cf999-fb4b-5e99-b208-917f67eaa2a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-100106"}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Quotient Rule to Compute a Limit Given a Graph"} {:db/id 17592186100621 :question/id #uuid "71b3f83c-33e6-5043-9215-7db7b4b12497" :question/math-academy-id "e-29" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186100953 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b0159149-010c-5bef-a28d-85c4c43f0586" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Quotient Rule to Compute a Limit Given a Graph"}] :question/problem "Find $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2} \dfrac{xf(x)+x^2}{2+f(x)}$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted below.

![](images/5b/5b29133a4e82b885aa3e20e423719564a61bfff5b33472addf5036d3a18efd3c.png)" :question/worked-solution "Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 2)(xf(x) + x^{2})/(2 + f(x)) &= (lim_(x → 2)(xf(x) + x^{2}))/(lim_(x → 2)(2 + f(x)))
\end{aligned}
$$

We find from the graph that

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 2} f(x)=3
$$

Calculating the limits of the numerator and denominator separately, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 2)(xf(x) + x^{2}) &= 2(3) + 2^{2} = 10, \\
lim_(x → 2)(2 + f(x)) &= 2 + 3 = 5
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the quotient of these limits, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
lim_(x → 2)(xf(x) + x^{2})/(2 + f(x)) &= (lim_(x → 2)(xf(x) + x^{2}))/(lim_(x → 2)(2 + f(x))) \\
&= \frac{10}{5} \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186101241 :question/id #uuid "567477b4-0e84-5ce6-8417-768895c7e8ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-17281"} {:db/id 17592186101242 :question/id #uuid $$
{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2f(x)}{3{x}^{2}}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to 1}(-2f(x))}{{lim}_{x\to 1}3{x}^{2}}.
$$

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}(-2f(x))=-2(6)=-12
$$

and

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}3{x}^{2}=3(1)^{2}=3.
$$

Taking the quotient of these limits, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2f(x)}{3{x}^{2}} & =\frac{{lim}_{x\to 1}(-2f(x))}{{lim}_{x\to 1}3{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-12}{3} \\  & =-4\,.\end{aligned}

\mathcal{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}bc\sin{A},
$$

where $\angle{A}$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB, \\ b & =AC=12\text{ cm}, \\ m∠A & ={45}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\sin{45^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2},
$$

we can calculate $c=AB,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ 24\sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 12\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘} \\ 24\sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 12\cdot c\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\ 24\cancel{\sqrt{2}} & =3\cancel{\sqrt{2}}c \\ 24 & =3c \\ c & =8\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Area of a Quadrilateral"}] :question/problem "Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD?$

![](images/bc/bc9f32a9c0e8b042498a72e808a29274bd505e786d8ec43d0e0bc9888fdf6e44.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is the sum of the areas of the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ADC$ (see the illustration below).

![](images/ac/acd2e923a65d0821cd59ed8b8274ceb5fc38def896467e37c8b1d454f958699e.png)

 First, we find the area for $\triangle ABC,$ and get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABC} & =\frac{1}{2}(42)(35)\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘} \\  & =735\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘} \\  & ≈432.022\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Now we find the area for $\triangle ADC,$ and get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ADC} & =\frac{1}{2}(20)(18)\operatorname{sin}⁡{80}^{∘} \\  & =180\operatorname{sin}⁡{80}^{∘} \\  & ≈177.265\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD.$ We get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ABC}+{A}_{ADC} \\  & =432.022+177.265 \\  & ≈609\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $609.$"} {:db/id 17592186106087 :question/id #uuid "0dab1268-d1c2-5547-a6e5-c75f85a4f239" :question/math-academy-id ![](images/6e/6e070d26915bcb11118f5a23f36b80038d5dd865e32a8517a12c10939ca02f0b.png)

First, we find the area of $△ABD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot 8\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{85}^{∘} \\  & =24\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{85}^{∘} \\  & ≈23.908\,7,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Now we find the area of $△BCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{BCD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 14\cdot 16\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{36.4}^{∘} \\  & =112\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{36.4}^{∘} \\  & ≈66.462\,9,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ABD}+{A}_{BCD} \\  & ≈23.908\,7+66.462\,9 \\  & ≈90.371\,6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $90.$"} {:db/id 17592186295111 :question/id #uuid "1e17900e-d26f-58a6-baab-ca3dab29afb6" :question/math-academy-id $$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ACD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot DA\cdot DC\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡D \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(25)(32)\operatorname{sin}⁡{70}^{∘} \\  & =400\operatorname{sin}⁡{70}^{∘} \\  & =375.877... \\  & ≈376\,{\text{cm}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

The difference of the areas of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ and $\triangle ACD$ gives the area of $\triangle ABC.$ Therefore, 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABC} & ={A}_{ACD}-{A}_{ABCD} \\  & =376-300 \\  & =76\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186106088 :question/id #uuid "157038e6-e68d-5ec0-b464-27301542d833" :question/math-academy-id "q-18188"} {:db/id 17592186106089 :question/id #uuid If the area of ​​the window is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}\,\textrm{m}^2$, what is the diameter of the corresponding circle?

![](images/1f/1f22d702fbf4504b14787f71a45e3821cdac6d3a90acb40c1a49ce498d28f986.png)" :question/worked-solution "The area of the circle is four times the area of the quarter section. So,

$$
\mathcal{A}=4\cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} =2\pi\,\textrm{m}^2
$$

The formula for the area of a circle is

$$
\mathcal{A}=\pi r^2
$$

, where $r$ is the radius. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= πr^{2} \\
2π &= πr^{2} \\
2π &= πr^{2} \\
2 &= r^{2} \\
r &= \sqrt{2}m
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the diameter is

$$
d=2\cdot r= 2\cdot \sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}\,\textrm{m}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120481 :question/id #uuid "fe87ed3a-4970-5077-bc59-f7b4984f84bb" :question/math-academy-id "q-53577"} {:db/id 17592186120485 :question/id #uuid "318c87b8-6c1f-58e1-bd75-19e907aa4de9" :question/math-academy-id "q-53639"} {:db/id 17592186119861 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119676 :question/id #uuid "78a454c8-c08b-5c4a-8ff6-cd093296c6d9" :question/math-academy-id "e-6804"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f1740fa9-50b1-5fad-9f99-31820dd77067" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048187}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120484 :question/id #uuid "2de757fe-4880-549b-b86b-48d7bc99fe1a" :question/math-academy-id "q-53585"} {:db/id 17592186120487 :question/id #uuid "ae47c864-e0fd-576d-a267-2b9c14c59bcd" :question/math-academy-id "q-53642"} {:db/id 17592186233302 :question/id #uuid "dd94009d-7285-58c6-9df1-2341d32131ef" :question/math-academy-id "q-122326"} {:db/id 17592186518101 :question/id #uuid "0207e47c-2942-5ced-8414-95264c8bde68" :question/math-academy-id "q-5658"}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Radius or Diameter of a Circle Given the Area"} {:db/id 17592186119676 :question/id #uuid "78a454c8-c08b-5c4a-8ff6-cd093296c6d9" :question/math-academy-id "e-6804" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186119861 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f1740fa9-50b1-5fad-9f99-31820dd77067" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Radius or Diameter of a Circle Given the Area"}] :question/problem "Given that the area of a circle is $22\pi\,\textrm{cm}^2$, what is its radius?" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the area of a circle is

$$

![](images/90/90280dd78d285df5dc798c3ec90b7fb47a72414f2934d36885eb9d65fd7584fd.png)" :question/worked-solution "The orange juice in the carton creates a cube. Since the height of the juice is $9\,\textrm{cm}$, the side length of the cube is also $9\,\textrm{cm}$.

The height of $9 \: \textrm{cm}$ shown in the diagram represents a third of the carton's height. Therefore, the height of the carton is

$$
3 \cdot 9 = 27 \: \textrm{cm}
$$

The empty space in the carton is a rectangular prism that is $9\:\textrm{cm}$ long, $9\:\textrm{cm}$ wide, and

$$
27 - 9 = 18\:\textrm{cm}
$$

high.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V = lwh
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting

$$
l=9\,\textrm{cm}, \qquad w=9\,\textrm{cm}, \qquad h=18\,\textrm{cm}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
V = 9 \cdot 9 \cdot 18 = 1\,458\:\textrm{cm}^3
$$

Therefore, we conclude that there is $1\,458 \: \textrm{cm}^3$ of empty space in the carton."} {:db/id 17592186120088 :question/id #uuid "f9fb6d92-70dd-5c7f-9979-070fe590bd5f" $$
V=lwh,

l=5,\,w=3,\,h=3
$$

into the formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}V=5\cdot 3\cdot 3=45\,{\text{yd}}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The total volume of the ten units is

$$
45\cdot 10=450\,{\text{yd}}^{3}.
$$

Finally, to rent the storage units, each day the company must pay

$$
450\cdot $2=$900.

To convert the measure of an angle in radians to an equivalent measure in degrees, we multiply the measure in radians by

$$
\dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}
$$

This gives

$$
\left(\dfrac{2\pi} 5\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac {180^\circ} {\pi}\right) = 72^\circ
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{2\pi}{5}
$$

- For graphs I, II, and III, some horizontal lines intersect the curve more than once. So, these are not one-to-one functions. As a result, they are not invertible.

invertible?

- $x \in (-\infty, 2]$

- $x \in (0, \infty)$

- $x \in (-1,4]$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's graph the given function. The graph of the function $f(x)=|x-2|-2$ can be obtained in the following way:  

- Take the curve $y=|x|.$

- Translate it by $2$ units to the right,  to get $y= |x-2|.$

- Finally, translate $y= |x-2|$ by $2$ units down to get $f(x)=|x-2|-2.$

![](images/60/60c2601abfd3c4034991408f47b75c8cf70a1bccb72f73b2f9624a52d0ed7b42.png)

Now, remember that a function is invertible on a particular interval if and only if it's a one-to-one function on that interval. To determine the intervals on which the function is invertible, we use the horizontal line test. 

- The function $f(x)$ is invertible on the interval $x\in(-\infty,2].$  Indeed, on this interval, any horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line.

![](images/45/45b0cdd26280d9379a449af41edbc9e69dd9d76f3b4116d938fbe708c21f6f29.png)

- The function $f(x)$ is not invertible on any of the intervals $x\in(0,\infty)$ and $x \in (-1,4].$ On these intervals, some horizontal lines will intersect the curve more than once.

![](images/55/55b8483c59362d3a59dfd269db74f2c5f17a97cee1f25c896ece16890d80bd42.png)

  

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186048598} {:db/id 17592186049474} {:db/id 17592186049620} {:db/id 17592186049716} {:db/id 17592186513242} {:db/id 17592186125195 :question/id - Finally, translate $y=|x-4|$ by $2$ units up to get $f(x)=|x-4|+2.$

![](images/56/56956d0f23ae6828098507712fd00525dc4f114a195716dc16e63d8475e9c143.png)

A function is invertible on a particular interval if and only if it's a one-to-one function on that interval. To determine the intervals on which the function is invertible, we use the horizontal line test. 

- The function $f(x)$ is invertible on the interval $x\in (-\infty ,3).$  Indeed, on this interval, any horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line.

- The function $f(x)$ is not invertible on any of the intervals $x\in (1,\infty )$  and $(-\infty ,5].$ On each of these intervals, some horizontal lines will intersect the curve more than once.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186323741 :question/id #uuid "aef31e6b-2918-5842-b5c4-348781827064" :question/math-academy-id "q-36010"} {:db/id 17592186335885 :question/id The resulting polygon is $A'B'C'D'$. Which of the following statements are true?

1. $A$ coincides with $A'$
2. $\angle ACB \cong \angle A'C'B'$
3. $AB = A'B'$" :question/worked-solution "The given transformation is a rotation of $\alpha$ counterclockwise about the point $A$, which is a rigid motion. Rigid motions preserve the distances between all points and all angle measures.

![](images/73/73d6148ffe8d269f7846cf95679cddef30e058380aef6546fb8bd7577d9e9b80.png)

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true. Under the action of the transformation, the point $A$ is left unchanged. Therefore, $A=A'$.
- Statement II is true. Under the action of the transformation, the measures of all corresponding angles are preserved. Therefore, $\angle{ACB}\cong \angle{A'C'B'}$.
- Statement III is true. Under the action of the transformation, the distance between all corresponding points is preserved. Therefore, $AB = A'B'$.

- Translations
- Rotations
- Reflections

With that in mind, let's examine each of the transformations in turn.

- Transformation I is a translation of $3$ units to the left and $4$ units down. This is a rigid motion. So, it maps every polygon to a congruent polygon.
- Transformation II is a dilation of scale factor $2$. This is *not* a rigid motion. So, it does not map every polygon to a congruent polygon.
- Transformation III is a reflection in the line $y=x$. This is a rigid motion. So, it maps every polygon to a congruent polygon.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186048208} {:db/id 17592186049034} {:db/id 17592186050093} {:db/id 17592186050239} {:db/id 17592186134457 :question/id #uuid :question/problem "Find the equation for the common ratio of the geometric sequence whose $4$th term is $6$ and whose $9$th term is $192$." :question/worked-solution "The formula for the $n$th term of a geometric sequence is given by

$$
a_n = a_1r^{n-1}
$$

Applying this formula with $n=4$ and $n=9$, respectively, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{4} &= a_{1}r^{4 - 1} = a_{1}r^{3}, \\
a_{9} &= a_{1}r^{9 - 1} = a_{1}r^{8}
\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $a_4 = 6$ and $a_9 = 192$, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
{a_{1}r^{3} = 6; a_{1}r^{8} = 192
$$

Finally, by dividing the second equation by the first, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a_{1}r^{8}}{a_{1}r^{3}} &= \frac{192}{6} \\
\frac{a_{1}r^{8}}{a_{1}r^{3}} &= \frac{192}{6} \\
\frac{r^{8}}{r^{3}} &= 32 \\
r^{5} &= 32
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050067} {:db/id 17592186148112 :question/id #uuid "0db1c042-7d67-5885-8fb9-36082f73ad6e" :question/math-academy-id "q-64038"} {:db/id 17592186148113 :question/id #uuid "c06aba2d-2479-5cdf-8546-7f59fe49fc43" :question/math-academy-id "q-64039"} {:db/id 17592186147462 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147226 :question/id #uuid "9d8383ad-c617-5b01-8055-214a8c639f12" :question/math-academy-id "e-2175"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "631bc93f-4596-526f-9652-f35137b60883" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049066} {:db/id 17592186050511} {:db/id 17592186050828}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147752 :question/id #uuid "efcbcd49-2437-59f8-829f-a86a1e76bba0" :question/math-academy-id "q-250935"} {:db/id 17592186148111 :question/id #uuid "a23f58d3-b672-5145-bfda-f50d7c8f3203" :question/math-academy-id "q-64030"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Common Ratio Using a Formula Given Two Non-Consecutive Terms"} {:db/id 17592186147226 :question/id #uuid "9d8383ad-c617-5b01-8055-214a8c639f12" :question/math-academy-id "e-2175" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186147462 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "631bc93f-4596-526f-9652-f35137b60883" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Common Ratio Using a Formula Given Two Non-Consecutive Terms"}] :question/problem "Find the common ratio of the geometric sequence whose fourth term is $2$ and whose seventh term is $-686$." :question/worked-solution "To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms $a_m$ and $a_n$, we use the formula

$$
r^{n-m} = \dfrac{a_n}{a_m}
$$

In this case, we're given $a_7 = -686$ and $a_4 = 2$. Substituting $n=7$ and $m=4$ into the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{7 - 4} &= \frac{a_{7}}{a_{4}} \\
r^{3} &= \frac{-686}{2} \\
r^{3} &= -343
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by solving the equation for $r$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{3} &= -343 \\
r^{3} &= (-7)^{3} \\

$$

$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
x^2 - 2x - 15 = 0 \quad \textrm{and} \quad e^{x-1}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $x^2 - 2x - 15  = 0$ can be factored as

$$
(x+3)(x-5)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-3,5.$

- The equation $e^{x-1}=0$ has no solutions because $e^{x-1}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

:question/problem "What is the product of solutions of the equation $9x^2\cdot 3^{x+1} = 16\cdot 3^{x+1}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}\cdot {3}^{x+1} & =16\cdot {3}^{x+1} \\ 9{x}^{2}\cdot {3}^{x+1}-16\cdot {3}^{x+1} & =0 \\ (9{x}^{2}-16){3}^{x+1} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
9x^2 - 16  = 0 \quad \textrm{and} \quad 3^{x+1}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $9x^2 - 16=0$ can be factored as

$$
(3x+4)(3x-4) = 0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-\dfrac{4}{3},\dfrac{4}{3}.$

- The equation $3^{x+1}=0$ has no solutions because $3^{x+1}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, the original equation has the solutions $x=-\dfrac{4}{3},\dfrac{4}{3},$ and their product is $\left( -\dfrac{4}{3} \right) \cdot \dfrac{4}{3} = -\dfrac{16}{9}.$"} {:db/id 17592186517474} $$
(2x+3)(2x-1)=0,
$$

- The equation ${e}^{5x}=0$ has no solutions because ${e}^{5x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

$$
f(x)=0
$$

$$
\sqrt[3]{4x-5} - 3 = 0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt[3]{4x - 5} - 3 &= 0 \\
\sqrt[3]{4x - 5} &= 3 \\
(\sqrt[3]{4x - 5})^{3} &= 3^{3} \\
4x - 5 &= 27 \\
4x &= 32 \\
x &= 8
\end{aligned}
$$

"4b042103-9e24-53d9-bc20-80a9a90d191b" :knowledge-point/title "Writing the Equation of a Parabola in Vertex Form"}] :question/problem "Write the parabola $y=x^2-20x+20$ in vertex form." :question/worked-solution "To express the equation of the parabola in vertex form, we need to complete the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= x^{2} - 20x + 20 \\
&= x^{2} - 2 \cdot 10 \cdot x + 20 \\
&= x^{2} - 2 \cdot 10 \cdot x + 10^{2} - 10^{2} + 20 \\
&= (x^{2} - 2 \cdot 10 \cdot x + 10^{2}) - 10^{2} + 20 \\
&= (x - 10)^{2} - 10^{2} + 20 \\
&= (x - 10)^{2} - 100 + 20 \\
&= (x - 10)^{2} - 80
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, expressed in vertex form, the equation of the parabola is

$$
y=(x-10)^2 - 80
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049622} {:db/id 17592186050372} {:db/id 17592186172312 :question/id #uuid "457abe79-0f38-58a6-8bed-2b1f2cf63c0b" :question/math-academy-id "q-13443"} {:db/id 17592186172479 :question/id #uuid "88af7275-a3a1-5004-9650-033183a2e331" :question/math-academy-id "q-249946"} {:db/id 17592186172137 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171743 :question/id #uuid "108ee1b6-2266-5956-b06d-4f4092fdee57" :question/math-academy-id "e-1469"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a23a10c1-a091-55bb-98a6-7718e46d841b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186051078}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172441 :question/id #uuid "31f473c4-882e-5064-9c97-feb36b895be7" :question/math-academy-id "q-220346"} {:db/id 17592186172557 :question/id #uuid "73773ba9-718f-5371-a794-8fd45abba00e" :question/math-academy-id "q-46113"} {:db/id 17592186234061 :question/id #uuid "7b10f970-f0c0-5c1c-948f-9f92d7941265" :question/math-academy-id "q-46167"}] :knowledge-point/title "Writing the Equation of a Parabola With Leading Coefficients in Vertex Form"} {:db/id 17592186171743 :question/id #uuid "108ee1b6-2266-5956-b06d-4f4092fdee57" :question/math-academy-id "e-1469" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186172137 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a23a10c1-a091-55bb-98a6-7718e46d841b" :knowledge-point/title "Writing the Equation of a Parabola With Leading Coefficients in Vertex Form"}] :question/problem "Write the equation of the parabola $y=2x^2 - 12x + 2$ in vertex form." :question/worked-solution "To express the equation of the parabola in vertex form, we need to complete the square.

First, we take out a factor of $2$ from the entire expression:

$$
2x^2 - 12x + 2 = 2(x^2 - 6x + 1)
$$

Now, we complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - 6x + 1 &= x^{2} - 2 \cdot 3 \cdot x + 1 \\
&= x^{2} - 2 \cdot 3 \cdot x + 3^{2} - 3^{2} + 1 \\
&= (x^{2} - 2 \cdot 3 \cdot x + 3^{2}) - 3^{2} + 1 \\
&= (x - 3)^{2} - 3^{2} + 1 \\
&= (x - 3)^{2} - 9 + 1 \\
&= (x - 3)^{2} - 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2(x^{2} - 6x + 1) &= 2((x - 3)^{2} - 8) \\
&= 2(x - 3)^{2} - 16
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, expressed in vertex form, the equation of the parabola is

$$
y=2(x-3)^2 - 16
$$"} {:db/id 17592186051078} {:db/id 17592186172441 :question/id #uuid "31f473c4-882e-5064-9c97-feb36b895be7" :question/math-academy-id "q-220346"} {:db/id 17592186172557 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The curve $y=4{x}^{2}-24x+24$ can be written as $y=a(x+b)^{2}+c.$ Calculate $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "To express the equation of the parabola in vertex form, we need to complete the square. 

First, we take out a factor of $4$ from the entire expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-24x+24 & =4({x}^{2}-6x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-6x+6 & = \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 3\cdot x+6 & = \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+6 & = \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2})-{3}^{2}+6 & = \\ (x-3)^{2}-{3}^{2}+6 & = \\ (x-3)^{2}-9+6 & = \\ (x-3)^{2}-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}^{2}-6x+6) & = \\ 4((x-3)^{2}-3) & = \\ 4(x-3)^{2}-12\end{aligned}
$$

So,  $a+b+c=4+(-3)+(-12)=-11.$"} {:db/id 17592186172138 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171825 :question/id #uuid "0a48df2c-c48e-5862-884f-3768abfbe5df" :question/math-academy-id "e-7478"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3d374538-dedf-5a73-9cec-d30491eb1393" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172480 :question/id #uuid "6fd4afc5-cd79-5856-a4b9-76c4fe2c04b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-249979"} {:db/id 17592186172558 :question/id #uuid "14bd26f2-ad1f-5e72-a20e-872560cd413d" :question/math-academy-id "q-46163"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Equation of a Parabola Given Its Vertex and Leading Coefficient"} {:db/id 17592186171825 :question/id #uuid "0a48df2c-c48e-5862-884f-3768abfbe5df" :question/math-academy-id "e-7478" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186172138 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3d374538-dedf-5a73-9cec-d30491eb1393" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Equation of a Parabola Given Its Vertex and Leading Coefficient"}] :question/problem "Find the equation of the parabola whose vertex is $(1, 2)$ and whose leading coefficient is $5$." :question/worked-solution "Remember that the vertex form of a parabola is

$$
y = a(x-h)^2 + k
$$

where $(h,k)$ are the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola, and $a$ is the leading coefficient.

Substituting

$$
(h,k) = (1,2)
$$

and $a=5$ into the above and then expanding and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= 5(x - 1)^{2} + 2 \\
&= 5(x^{2} - 2x + 1) + 2 \\
&= 5x^{2} - 10x + 5 + 2 \\
&= 5x^{2} - 10x + 7
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
y = 5x^2-10x+7
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172480 :question/id #uuid "6fd4afc5-cd79-5856-a4b9-76c4fe2c04b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-249979"} {:db/id 17592186172558 :question/id #uuid According to the regression model, what is the residual for the highlighted datapoint?" :question/worked-solution "The residual equals the difference between the actual value of the dependent variable and the value estimated using the linear regression model:

$$
\textrm{Residual} = \text{Actual} - \textrm{Estimated}
$$

The highlighted datapoint has coordinates $(82,70)$. So, our actual value is $y=70$.

On the other hand, the point on the regression line that corresponds to $x=82$ has the $y$-coordinate $65$. So, our estimated value is

$$
\widehat{y}=65
$$

![](images/99/99e3741f602802e636e2e49ef755954343079b8c0d98453dac9364ddc08ef16f.png)

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}
Residual &= Actual - Estimated \\
&= y - y^(^) \\
&= 70 - 65 \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the residual is $5$."} {:db/id 17592186049868} {:db/id 17592186176341 :question/id #uuid "dd98bac0-93e8-506d-a8ba-d1595548f912" :question/math-academy-id "q-134267"} {:db/id 17592186176342 :question/id #uuid "e312e8e0-12d2-524c-8d6c-c3bb62aee103" :question/math-academy-id "q-134276"} {:db/id 17592186176034 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175889 :question/id #uuid "cb2190d0-5150-53ff-b7ab-ed364611bc8f" :question/math-academy-id "e-9718"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0286d36b-217f-52e4-8580-e031b6dea31e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050210}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176339 :question/id #uuid "efe63102-9d28-56ff-a954-0f7f3b632bf3" :question/math-academy-id "q-134256"} {:db/id 17592186176340 :question/id #uuid "a189cf42-a35d-541c-8fa9-b13012c26ed3" :question/math-academy-id "q-134266"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Residuals Using the Regression Line Equation"} {:db/id 17592186175889 :question/id #uuid "cb2190d0-5150-53ff-b7ab-ed364611bc8f" :question/math-academy-id "e-9718" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186176034 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0286d36b-217f-52e4-8580-e031b6dea31e" :knowledge-point/title "Computing Residuals Using the Regression Line Equation"}] :question/problem "Consider the data sets $x$ and $y$ of paired observations. The equation of the corresponding linear regression line for this data is
$y=0.5x+7$.
According to the model, what is the residual at $x=6$ if the actual value of $y$ corresponding to this value of $x$ is $12$?" :question/worked-solution "The residual equals the difference between the actual value of the dependent variable and the value estimated using the linear regression model:

$$
\textrm{Residual} = \text{Actual} - \textrm{Estimated}
$$

First, we compute the predicted value using our linear regression model:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^(^) &= 0.5x + 7 \\
&= 0.5(6) + 7 \\
&= 10
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the residual is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Residual &= Actual - Estimated \\
&= y - y^(^) \\
&= 12 - 10 \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050210} {:db/id 17592186176339 :question/id #uuid "efe63102-9d28-56ff-a954-0f7f3b632bf3" :question/math-academy-id "q-134256"} {:db/id 17592186176340 :question/id #uuid "a189cf42-a35d-541c-8fa9-b13012c26ed3" :question/math-academy-id "q-134266"} {:db/id 17592186176035 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175890 :question/id #uuid "3b40900e-ca06-5951-8261-aa13d8f966ce" :question/math-academy-id "e-9719"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aa97e57a-70d8-5708-8b7d-fa05604a3f88" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176343 :question/id #uuid "d4f49124-81ec-5f2d-b275-feeb960c2f73" :question/math-academy-id "q-134284"} {:db/id 17592186176344 :question/id #uuid "7ae43775-06ac-519f-ac5d-57c73d122d92" :question/math-academy-id "q-134285"} {:db/id 17592186233432 :question/id #uuid "510cace3-4d24-50e7-9ee2-e819b9c603a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-134815"}] :knowledge-point/title "Interpreting Residual Plots"} {:db/id 17592186175890 :question/id #uuid "3b40900e-ca06-5951-8261-aa13d8f966ce" :question/math-academy-id "e-9719" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186176035 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aa97e57a-70d8-5708-8b7d-fa05604a3f88" :knowledge-point/title "Interpreting Residual Plots"}] :question/problem "![](images/7c/7c7bf33ee8878c6dc8e33622a5abe79a068b483ed19c0e177ecea31ab34b8777.png)

2. The residuals appear to be randomly scattered about the horizontal axis (there are no obvious trends).
3. This linear regression is probably a good fit for the data." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The residual equals the actual value minus the estimated value:

- Statement III is false. Since the residuals are *not* randomly scattered above and below the horizontal axis, our regression line is *not* a good fit for the given data.

The residual plot above was constructed after fitting a linear regression model on a set of bivariate numerical data $(x,y).$
Which of the following statements are true?

I. When $x=8,$ the regression equation overestimates the value of $y.$

II. The residuals appear to be randomly scattered about the horizontal axis (there are no obvious trends).

III. This linear regression is probably a good fit for the data." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The residual equals the actual value minus the estimated value:

$$
\text{Residual}=\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated}
$$

 
From the plot, the residual at $x=8$ is negative. So, we have that $\text{Actual}<\text{Estimated},$ and therefore the model overestimates  this data point.

- Statement II is false. The plot shows the residuals tend to decrease as $x$ increases. So, there is a trend, as shown below.

![](images/0b/0bb186e7b1c1923e7e8b2776b202b1dcd9b930c56583199964e47530805d246d.png)

- Statement III is false. Since the residuals are *not* randomly scattered above and below the horizontal axis, our regression line is *not* a good fit for the given data.

Expression"}] :question/problem "Write $2 + \dfrac{2}{k}$ as a single fraction." :question/worked-solution "Using the fact that

$$
2=\dfrac 2 1
$$

we can write the expression as

$$
\dfrac 2 1 + \dfrac{2}{k}
$$

In order to add the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. So, we put both fractions over a common denominator of $k$ by multiplying the top and bottom of the first fraction by $k$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2}{1} + \frac{2}{k} &=  \\
\frac{k}{k} \cdot \frac{2}{1} + \frac{2}{k} &=  \\
&= \frac{2k}{k} + \frac{2}{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we add the fractions and simplify the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2k}{k} + \frac{2}{k} &=  \\
\frac{2k + 2}{k} &=  \\
&= (2(k + 1))/(k)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050462} {:db/id 17592186050575} {:db/id 17592186180182 :question/id #uuid "c4906f3f-5058-5671-b3a5-090c5552dbcf" :question/math-academy-id "q-41566"} {:db/id 17592186180183 :question/id #uuid "65698589-f97d-56e6-8561-436b3f3f5011" :question/math-academy-id "q-41574" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "43113724-4737-55bd-be10-ea13f354c498" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{n+4}{4n}" :db/id 17592186324512} {:answer/id #uuid "557c2210-cde2-5a90-ab2d-278d391fa572" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{n+4}{n}" :db/id 17592186324681} {:answer/id #uuid "7c80d65a-f4b4-5976-85e0-2d42b91e04f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4(n+1)}{n}" :db/id 17592186325018} {:answer/id #uuid "86d696a3-51f6-5c74-b60a-ee777cf766f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2(n+1)}{n}" :db/id 17592186325119} {:answer/id #uuid "a5c3cf18-f2f8-5303-b271-47d390e13977" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4n+1}{4n}" :db/id 17592186325381}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325018} :answer-field/id #uuid "b3a0ac12-5ec7-59fe-bcab-532f6789e555" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326544}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Write $4+\frac{4}{n}$ as a single fraction." :question/worked-solution "Using the fact that $4=\frac{4}{1},$ we can write the expression as

$$

Finally, we add the fractions and simplify the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4n}{n}+\frac{4}{n} & = \\ \frac{4n+4}{n} & = \\ \frac{4(n+1)}{n}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186247331 :question/id #uuid "db256712-a567-5c31-aac9-855b317092f8" :question/math-academy-id "q-113217"} {:db/id 17592186247332 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{q} + \frac{1}{p + 1} &=  \\
\frac{p + 1}{p + 1} \cdot \frac{1}{q} + \frac{q}{q} \cdot \frac{1}{p + 1} &=  \\

&= (p + q + 1)/((p + 1)q)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180184 :question/id #uuid "ab19be5e-b60d-54d2-96bb-f15d6904d9b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-41577"} {:db/id 17592186180262 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4y}{x-6}+\frac{2y}{2x+3} & = \\ \frac{2x+3}{2x+3}\cdot \frac{4y}{x-6}+\frac{x-6}{x-6}\cdot \frac{2y}{2x+3} & = \\ \frac{4y(2x+3)}{(x-6)(2x+3)}+\frac{2y(x-6)}{(x-6)(2x+3)} & = \\ \frac{4y(2x+3)+2y(x-6)}{(x-6)(2x+3)} & = \\ \frac{8xy+12y+2xy-12y}{(x-6)(2x+3)} & = \\ \frac{10xy}{(x-6)(2x+3)}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & =\frac{x+1}{3x}-\frac{2y}{6y+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to put the fractions over a common denominator of $3x(6y+1),$ since there are no common factors in either denominator that we can exploit. 

To do this, we multiply the top and bottom of the first fraction by $6y+1,$ and the top and bottom of the second fraction by $3x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & =\frac{x+1}{3x}-\frac{2y}{6y+1} \\  & =\frac{6y+1}{6y+1}\cdot \frac{x+1}{3x}-\frac{3x}{3x}\cdot \frac{2y}{6y+1} \\  & =\frac{(6y+1)(x+1)}{3x(6y+1)}-\frac{3x(2y)}{3x(6y+1)} \\  & =\frac{(6y+1)(x+1)-3x(2y)}{3x(6y+1)} \\  & =\frac{6yx+x+6y+1-6xy}{3x(6y+1)} \\  & =\frac{x+6y+1}{3x(6y+1)}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048163} {:db/id 17592186048390} {:db/id 17592186048867} {:db/id 17592186049470} {:db/id 17592186049748} {:db/id 17592186050232} {:db/id 17592186050640} {:db/id 17592186048796 2. Stretch it by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $y$-axis
3. Translate it to the right by $4$ units

What is the final function expression after applying all the transformations?" :question/worked-solution "To find the expression, let's apply each of the transformations in turn.

1. Translating the graph of $y=f(x)$ up by $2$ units is equivalent to adding $2$ to the function expression. Applying this transformation, we obtain $y=f(x)+2$.
2. Stretching the graph of $y=f(x)+2$ by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $y$-axis is equivalent to multiplying the function expression by $5$. Applying this transformation, we obtain $y=5\big(f(x)+2 \big) = 5f(x)+10$.
3. Translating the graph of $y=5f(x)+10$ by $4$ units to the right is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $(x-4)$. Applying this transformation, we obtain $y =5f(x-4)+10$.

Therefore, the final function expression is

$$
y=5f(x-4)+10
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048186} {:db/id 17592186184859 :question/id #uuid "6b8945d2-4adf-5f3b-b405-7b670dac6d6d" :question/math-academy-id "q-87314"} {:db/id 17592186184865 :question/id #uuid "9f8e67ce-9f90-59ec-829f-0e60479433bc" :question/math-academy-id "q-87477"} {:db/id 17592186184227 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186184133 :question/id #uuid "afb9f795-d566-52e9-9b92-2046918e5d73" :question/math-academy-id "e-9988"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c76594da-4831-56c4-8c49-68349ba62a19" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184855 :question/id #uuid "fd5412ff-e9f8-58f0-b90b-ffbc0f61ca59" :question/math-academy-id "q-87045"} {:db/id 17592186184858 :question/id #uuid "ff1f2d2a-0b8f-5d07-a554-0be569e8a705" :question/math-academy-id "q-87312"} {:db/id 17592186233460 :question/id #uuid "3d424faa-a830-5c69-a1d8-32908ad96638" :question/math-academy-id "q-141752"}] :knowledge-point/title "Applying Several Transformations: Horizontal Stretch Followed By Horizontal Shift Inside Parentheses"} {:db/id 17592186184133 :question/id #uuid "afb9f795-d566-52e9-9b92-2046918e5d73" :question/math-academy-id "e-9988" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186184227 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c76594da-4831-56c4-8c49-68349ba62a19" :knowledge-point/title "Applying Several Transformations: Horizontal Stretch Followed By Horizontal Shift Inside Parentheses"}] :question/problem "Given the graph of $y=f(x)$, we apply the following transformations in the order given:

defined for $x >1$. Find $f^{-1}(x)$." :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = \dfrac{4}{(x-1)^2}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{4}{(y-1)^2}
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= (4)/((y - 1)^{2}) \\
x \cdot (y - 1)^{2} &= 4 \\
(y - 1)^{2} &= \frac{4}{x} \\
\sqrt{(y - 1)^{2}} &= \sqrt{\frac{4}{x}} \\
\mid y - 1 \mid &= \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}} \\
y - 1 &= \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}} \\
y &= \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}} + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that for $y > 1$, we have

$$
\mid y-1 \mid = y-1
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}} + 1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048963} {:db/id 17592186049461} {:db/id 17592186049636} {:db/id 17592186050383} {:db/id 17592186193007 :question/id #uuid "3c59175d-f52e-5041-89a5-4b75797aab41" inverse of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{2-x}{x+3}$." :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = \dfrac{2-x}{x+3}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{2-y}{y+3}
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{2 - y}{y + 3} \\
x(y + 3) &= 2 - y \\
xy + 3x &= 2 - y \\
xy + y &= 2 - 3x \\
y(x + 1) &= 2 - 3x \\
y &= \frac{2 - 3x}{x + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{2-3x}{x+1}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186051079} {:db/id 17592186193009 :question/id #uuid "3fbadf4f-ad61-5c64-abef-b812903e691b" :question/math-academy-id "q-148297"} {:db/id 17592186193020 :question/id #uuid $f(x) = \dfrac{kx + 6}{x-4}, \qquad x\neq 4$
has an inverse function given by
$f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{4x+6}{x-2}, \qquad x\neq 2$.
What is the value of $k$?" :question/worked-solution "To find $f^{-1}(x)$, we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y{:}$

$$
y = \dfrac{kx + 6}{x-4}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x = \dfrac{ky+6}{y-4}
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{ky + 6}{y - 4} \\
x(y - 4) &= ky + 6 \\
xy - 4x &= ky + 6 \\
xy - ky &= 4x + 6 \\
y(x - k) &= 4x + 6 \\
y &= \frac{4x + 6}{x - k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is

$$
f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{4x+6}{x-k}
$$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k=2$."} {:db/id 17592186193010 :question/id #uuid "08d61d78-0894-5a3b-a7fb-a0e5175e00e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-148298"} {:db/id "Consider the following system of equations.

To eliminate $a$, multiply the first equation by $44$
the second by $44$ and add the equations." :question/worked-solution "Notice that the coefficient of $a$ in the first equation is ${\color{red}{3}}$, while in the second equation it is ${\color{blue}{4}}$.

If we multiply the first equation by ${\color{blue}{4}}$ and the second equation by $-{\color{red}{3}}$, then the $a$-coefficient in the first and second equations will become $12$ and $-12$, and these will cancel when we add the equations.

$$
{(3a + 2b =-2) \cdot (4); (4a - 3b = 3) \cdot (-3)
$$

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable $a$ will be eliminated:

$$
\begin{aligned}
12a + 8b &= -8 \\
- 12a + 9b &= -9 \\
(8b + 9b) &= (-8 - 9) \\
17b &= -17
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is the following:

> *To eliminate $a$, multiply the first equation by $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}4}$, the second by $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-3}$, and add the equations.*"} {:db/id 17592186050190} {:db/id 17592186198909 :question/id #uuid "d499bb37-7b0a-5957-ad2b-37430ec45a4e" :question/math-academy-id "q-211003"} {:db/id 17592186198910 :question/id #uuid "e4f4ae99-1517-5eca-8202-ca942d72bcef" :question/math-academy-id "q-211005"} {:db/id 17592186198351 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198217 :question/id #uuid "68da240e-2c79-50d7-86dd-d203d01dcb32" :question/math-academy-id "e-14001"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9cf591e2-45d5-580c-9d46-c6a8645c0513" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198911 :question/id #uuid "a5b232e1-8ff4-5e67-a2e7-e6327dd0e4f8" :question/math-academy-id "q-211006"} {:db/id 17592186198912 :question/id #uuid "899f17d1-0e3f-59b7-ac0c-a07497128b0c" :question/math-academy-id "q-211007"}] :knowledge-point/title "Eliminating the Second Variable"} {:db/id 17592186198217 :question/id #uuid "68da240e-2c79-50d7-86dd-d203d01dcb32" :question/math-academy-id "e-14001" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186198351 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9cf591e2-45d5-580c-9d46-c6a8645c0513" :knowledge-point/title "Eliminating the Second Variable"}] :question/problem "Consider the following system of equations.

$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the $a$-coefficient in the first equation is $5,$ while in the second equation it is $-2.$ 

If we multiply the first equation by $2$ and the second equation by $5,$ then the $a$-coefficient in the first and second equations will become $10$ and $-10,$ and these will cancel when we add the equations.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(\,5a+4b=7\,)\,\times (2) \\ (\,-2a+6b=20\,)\,\times (5)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}10a+8b=14 \\ -10a+30b=100\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable $a$ will be eliminated:

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{10a}+8b & =14 \\ -\cancel{10a}+30b & =100 \\ (8b+30b) & =(14+100) \\ 38b & =114 \\ b & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $b=3.$ However, we still need to find $a.$ To do this, we substitute $b=3$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5a+4b & =7 \\ 5a+4(3) & =7 \\ 5a+12 & =7 \\ 5a & =-5 \\ a & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-1$ and $b=3,$ which can be written as $(-1,3).$"} {:db/id 17592186198353 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198219 :question/id #uuid "10d6a803-5114-5995-87c3-1b0e0e87a079" :question/math-academy-id "e-14004"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1fc5a393-5fcd-59c9-993b-d900b790e141" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198686 :question/id #uuid "e95e6a5b-70bc-5e33-839e-192ba0b136b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-170219"} {:db/id 17592186198997 :question/id #uuid "4ddaaf91-b033-575a-afb2-7aa11969b606" :question/math-academy-id "q-73052"}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving a System of Equations by Eliminating the Second Variable"} {:db/id 17592186198219 :question/id #uuid "10d6a803-5114-5995-87c3-1b0e0e87a079" :question/math-academy-id "e-14004" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186198353 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1fc5a393-5fcd-59c9-993b-d900b790e141" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a System of Equations by Eliminating the Second Variable"}] :question/problem "Find the solution $(x,y)$ to the system below by eliminating the variable $y$.

If we multiply the first equation by ${\color{blue}4}$ and the second equation by $-{\color{red}3}$, then the $y$-coefficient in the first and second equations will become $-12$ and $12$, and these will cancel when we add the equations.

$$
{(4x + 3y = 3) \cdot (4); (5x + 4y = 5) \cdot (-3)
$$

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable $y$ will be eliminated:

$$
\begin{aligned}
16x + 12y &= 12 \\
- 15x - 12y &= -15 \\
(16x - 15x) &= (12 - 15) \\
x &= -3
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=-3$. However, we still need to find $y$. To do this, we substitute $x=-3$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4x + 3y &= 3 \\
4(-3) + 3y &= 3 \\
- 12 + 3y &= 3 \\
3y &= 15 \\
y &= 5
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-3$ and $y=5$, which can be written as $(-3,5)$."} {:db/id 17592186198686 :question/id #uuid "e95e6a5b-70bc-5e33-839e-192ba0b136b8" $$

Give your answers to $2$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let us call $A$ the event "The student volunteers to play percussion" and $B$ the event "The student volunteers to play a wind instrument."

- The number of students who volunteer for percussion *only* is

so we write the number $17$ in the part of circle $A$ that does not overlap with circle $B$.

![](images/61/61cfe75b341ac014be0f81eb4e58ac605f7680c2f9fc0e08b443e6bd2c9cecb5.png)

- The number of students who volunteer for wind instruments *only* is
$15 - 3 = 12$,
so we write the number $12$ in the part of the circle $B$ that does not overlap with circle $A$.

![](images/b7/b704fa8f8e5f77e6188ccb8bbadbb2f3bf6ed8034897b8b1d205574da35030a5.png)

The total number of students who volunteered for percussion or wind instruments is

$$
3 + 17 + 12 = 32
$$

and there are $35$ students in total, so the number of remaining students is

$$
35 - 32 = 3
$$

To represent these $3$ students who did not volunteer for wind instruments or percussion, we write the number $3$ outside of the circles $A$ and $B$.

Therefore, our final Venn diagram looks as shown below:

![](images/1b/1b87d550b2adf6399f31a3c2e8ded4496a02058e904c8682c9c50d26f6ec6d50.png)

The shaded part of the Venn diagram corresponds to students who volunteered neither for percussion nor wind instruments. The probability that a randomly selected student is from this group is given by

$$
P(A'\cap B')=\dfrac{3}{35} \approx 0.09
$$

$$

Let's expand the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)(x+k) & ={x}^{2}+kx+3x+3k \\  & ={x}^{2}+(k+3)x+3k.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Since the equation is true for all values of $x,$ the expressions on both sides must be exactly the same. That means the product on the left-hand side must expand to match the right-hand side.

First, let's expand the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(ax-8)(x+b) & =a{x}^{2}+abx-8x-8b \\  & =a{x}^{2}+(ab-8)x-8b.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we equate the expanded form to the right-hand side:

$$
a{x}^{2}+(ab-8)x-8b=4{x}^{2}-32x+48.
$$

Now, we compare the coefficients of corresponding terms.

- Equating the coefficients of ${x}^{2},$ we get

$$
a=4.
$$

- Equating the constant terms, we get

$$
-8\cdot b=48⇒b=-6.
$$

Let's verify that values $a=4$ and $b=-6$ produce the correct linear coefficient:

$$
\begin{aligned}ab-8 & =4\cdot (-6)-8 \\  & =-24-8 \\  & =-32\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

which matches the coefficient of $x$ on the right-hand side. So, our solution is valid.

Finally, we compute the value of $a+b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =4+(-6) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048178} {:db/id 17592186048693} {:db/id 17592186048696} {:db/id 17592186049370} {:db/id 17592186050236} {:db/id 17592186050342} {:db/id 17592186050933} {:db/id 17592186048758 &= \frac{3 + \sqrt{a}}{9 - a}

:knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186213066 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "098734a8-c226-5bc7-b174-7c0d794e986c" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing Linear Functions Using Slope-Intercept Form"}] :question/problem "A linear function $g(x)$ gives the remaining mobile data, in gigabytes, on a monthly plan after $x$ days of continuous usage. There are $48$ GB remaining after $2$ days, and $30$ GB remaining after $5$ days. Which equation defines $g(x)$?" :question/worked-solution "The linear function modeling this situation is

$$
g(x) = mx + b
$$

We know two points on the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x_{1}, y_{1}) &= (2, 48) \\
(x_{2}, y_{2}) &= (5, 30)
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the given two points, we find the slope $m{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= \frac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}} \\
&= \frac{30 - 48}{5 - 2} \\
&= \frac{-18}{3} \\
&=-6
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the linear function is

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(x) &= mx + b \\
&=-6x + b
\end{aligned}
$$

To find the value of $b$, we substitute one of the points, say $(2, 48)$, into this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
48 &= -6 \cdot 2 + b \\
48 &= -12 + b \\
b &= 60
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the linear equation that defines $g(x)$ is

$$
g(x) = -6x + 60
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048217} {:db/id 17592186050216} {:db/id 17592186213544 :question/id #uuid "ea5f576e-7e2c-579f-9b09-887832fa06a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-292836"} {:db/id 17592186213557 :question/id #uuid "1a85616f-f6bb-5d8e-af01-fe90edfea9ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-293539"} {:db/id 17592186213067 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186212793 :question/id #uuid "604f7244-01c2-597e-9590-b7ab3965d816" :question/math-academy-id "e-18926"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b3da0835-3969-564f-b987-a019aca8fb55" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186213550 :question/id #uuid "381f7b0d-ee82-5dc5-8932-ec65db88b8a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-292875"} {:db/id 17592186213571 :question/id #uuid "36b81b99-08c9-5510-aec4-9db946ca6ef7" :question/math-academy-id "q-294209"}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing Functions From Tabular Data"} {:db/id 17592186212793 :question/id #uuid "604f7244-01c2-597e-9590-b7ab3965d816" :question/math-academy-id "e-18926" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186213067 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b3da0835-3969-564f-b987-a019aca8fb55" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing Functions From Tabular Data"}] :question/problem "| $x$ | $r(x)$ |
| --- | ---: |
| $6$ | $22$ |
| $9$ | $31$ |
| $12$ | $40$ |

Some values of the linear function $r$ are shown in the table above. Which of the following defines $r(x)$?" :question/worked-solution "Since $r$ is a linear function, we know it must be of the form

$$
r(x) = mx + b
$$

where

- $m$ is the slope, and
- $b$ is the $y$-intercept.

First, we find the slope using two points. For $x = 6$ and $x = 9$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= (r(x_{2}) - r(x_{1}))/(x_{2} - x_{1}) \\
&= \frac{31 - 22}{9 - 6} \\
&= \frac{9}{3} \\
&= 3
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the linear function is

$$
\begin{aligned}
r(x) &= mx + b \\
&= 3x + b
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the $y$-intercept using one point. For $x = 6$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
r(6) &= 3(6) + b \\
22 &= 18 + b \\
b &= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the linear equation that defines $r(x)$ is

$$
r(x) = 3x + 4
$$"} {:db/id 17592186213550 :question/id #uuid "381f7b0d-ee82-5dc5-8932-ec65db88b8a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-292875"} {:db/id 17592186213571 :question/id #uuid "36b81b99-08c9-5510-aec4-9db946ca6ef7" :question/math-academy-id "q-294209"} {:db/id 17592186213068 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186212789 :question/id #uuid "4fb71375-cea2-5364-b809-c844c462a1a9" :question/math-academy-id "e-18921"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "410a9971-d4c0-57ff-b936-58621a2313b5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049072} {:db/id 17592186050908}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186213545 :question/id #uuid "742ee3d0-d507-53a5-84ef-417daf52e33a" :question/math-academy-id "q-292837"} {:db/id 17592186213546 :question/id #uuid "eb5a05ab-0b72-5adf-9c8f-14be7bdfa741" :question/math-academy-id "q-292838"} {:db/id 17592186512876 :question/id #uuid "18899ab8-1919-5955-a40e-8e20033f8007" :question/math-academy-id "q-293604"}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing Functions With Alternative Domains"} {:db/id 17592186212789 :question/id #uuid "4fb71375-cea2-5364-b809-c844c462a1a9" :question/math-academy-id "e-18921" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186213068 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "410a9971-d4c0-57ff-b936-58621a2313b5" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing Functions With Alternative Domains"}] :question/problem "A theme park charges $\[math]65$ per person for the first $30$ people in a group and $\[/math]50$ for each additional person. Which function $C$ gives the total cost, in dollars, for a group of $g$ people, where $g \geq 30$?" :question/worked-solution "The total cost consists of two parts.

- For the first $30$ people, the park charges

$$
65 \times 30 = 1,950\,\,\textrm{dollars}
$$

- For the additional persons beyond $30$, the park charges

$$
50(g - 30)\,\,\textrm{dollars}
$$

Therefore, the total cost $C$, in dollars, for a group of $g$ people, where

$$
g\geq 30
$$

is

$$
\begin{aligned}
C(g) &= 1, 950 + 50(g - 30) \\
&= 1, 950 + 50g - 1, 500 \\
&= 50g + 450
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049072} {:db/id 17592186213545 :question/id #uuid "742ee3d0-d507-53a5-84ef-417daf52e33a" :question/math-academy-id "q-292837"} {:db/id 17592186213546 :question/id #uuid :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186084102 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084442 :tutorial/content "Suppose we roll a fair die. Then, the sample space $\mathcal S$ of this experiment is

$$
\mathcal{S} = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}
$$

Now, let's consider the event
$X = \{6\}$.
This means that $X$ is the event "the die lands on $6$." We know that

$$
P(X) = \dfrac{1}{6}
$$

because there are $6$ equally likely outcomes and only $1$ of those outcomes is a $6$.

We can represent the entire sample space $\mathcal S$, the event $X$, and its probability using a **Venn diagram**.

we wish to evaluate $\log_{4}9$, but our calculator only has a key for the common logarithm $\log$ (base $10$).

In such cases, we can use the **change of base formula**, which states that

$$
\log_a X = \dfrac {\log_b X} {\log_b a}
$$

It effectively allows us to change a logarithm from one base, $a$, to another, $b$. Note that $X$, $a$, and $b$ have to be all greater than zero and that

$$
a \ne 1
$$

$$
b \ne 1
$$

Using this formula, we can rewrite the logarithm from base $a=4$ to base $b=10$, to get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log_{4} 9 &= \frac{\log 9}{\log 4} \\
&\approx \frac{0.954242}{0.602059} \\
&= 1.585
\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :tutorial/id #uuid "bb104b87-e850-5cff-9826-fdd61c0287d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2797 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid transformation**.

Any combination of transformations made up of translation, rotation, reflection, and dilation will result in a similarity transformation.

To understand why this is true, remember:

- Rigid motions (rotation, reflection, and translation) do not change the lengths or angles of the original figure. They map polygons to congruent polygons. If two polygons are congruent, then they are similar.
- A dilation with scale factor $k$ multiplies all the lengths of the original shape by $k$ (leaving the angle measures unchanged), thereby producing a similar shape." :tutorial/id #uuid "622763c1-840b-5946-a1e7-feb59d8f0c89" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2315 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7ec1bc50-2134-5ed0-aa3d-e29348fd99e7" :step/math-academy-id 9647 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074720}} {:db/id 17592186074924 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073916 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073602 :question/id #uuid "54f05d2d-1137-5bc7-b56d-0215dc3895ad" :question/math-academy-id "e-2978"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d7545aba-d80b-58ab-9a56-25ad196da3ee" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074183} {:db/id 17592186074184}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Similarity Transformation Given a Polygon and Its Image"} :step/id #uuid "b8d1a4d2-47c1-5676-a5b1-d16b02e3ee67" :step/math-academy-id 9655 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074925}} {:db/id 17592186074925 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073917 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073603 :question/id #uuid "a75b57a8-4819-594a-9aa2-e35b54a68f6a" :question/math-academy-id "e-2993"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a8b5ef8e-6f13-5496-ae7f-c9fbaf3e25c7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074207} {:db/id 17592186074209} {:db/id 17592186234140} {:db/id 17592186234141} {:db/id 17592186516783} {:db/id 17592186516855}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Similarity Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "3698100e-df7d-5666-8520-aa605b0f8eca" :step/math-academy-id 9670}] :activity/title "Similarity Transformations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186073926} {:db/id 17592186074923 :step/content {:db/id 17592186074984 :tutorial/content "Any transformation that maps a polygon to a similar polygon is called a **similarity transformation**.

:question/math-academy-id "q-89714" :question/problem "A square $ABCD$ is translated by $3$ units to the left and $3$ units upward. If the resulting quadrilateral is $PQRS,$ which of the following statements must be true?

I. $ABCD∼PQRS$

II. $ABCD≅PQRS$

III. $\overset{―}{BC}≅\overset{―}{QR}$" :question/worked-solution "A similarity transformation is any transformation made up of rigid motions (rotations, reflections, and translations) and dilations. 

A similarity transformation will map any polygon to a similar polygon.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We are given a combination of translations. As a result, we obtain that 

$$
ABCD∼PQRS.
$$

- Statement II is true. Since our combined transformation consists of rigid motions only (namely, translations), the distance between all points is preserved under the transformation. Therefore,  we obtain that 

$$
ABCD≅PQRS.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since $ABCD≅PQRS,$ all corresponding sides must be congruent. Therefore, 

$$
\overset{―}{BC}≅\overset{―}{QR}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} :step/id #uuid "34047e62-3d93-591d-8a51-e16282e2c37f"} {:db/id 17592186516967 :step/content {:db/id 17592186516783 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "41f1557f-aa1b-5c6b-97f9-3183a0fdae13" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186516243} {:answer/id #uuid "5eeba46f-9dda-59a4-86da-d1ee0173c9ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186516317} {:answer/id #uuid "8861175f-b2e1-5165-afbc-bffd586e1f4b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186516397} {:answer/id #uuid "be0af016-3822-5b80-b2b9-b035f07b9902" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186516511} {:answer/id #uuid "c746c42b-4136-5b7a-8e70-85095e0c0424" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186516533}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186516511} :answer-field/id #uuid "f4eeffe0-d387-54ea-99bf-7c07fda39ad8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186516762}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1ea750dd-05b5-599b-a75b-1d40366d85dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-89161" :question/problem "Which of the following transformations map any polygon to a similar polygon?
